83204.q: What protects the space capsule from the great heat on the way back?
83204.e: When it enters the atmosphere, the outside of the capsule gets very hot. The heat shield on the underside protects the astronauts.
83204.m: The heat shield protects the capsule from the heat.

83205.q: What is it called when a space capsule attaches itself to the space station?
83205.e: The capsule moves very slowly up to the space station. Then it attaches itself there, which is called docking.
83205.m: Space capsules dock at the space station.

83206.q: What is the space capsule for astronauts from the company SpaceX called?
83206.e: Since 2020 astronauts have flown to the space station in the Crew Dragon capsule.
83206.m: Crew Dragon takes astronauts to the space station.

83207.q: What slows down a space capsule just before landing?
83207.e: Large parachutes open and slow the capsule down. That way it lands gently.
83207.m: Parachutes slow down the space capsule.

83208.q: Where did the American space capsules land after the flight to the Moon?
83208.e: The American Moon capsules landed in the sea with parachutes. Ships then picked up the astronauts.
83208.m: The Moon capsules landed in the sea.

83209.q: Where does the Russian space capsule usually land when it brings astronauts back from the space station?
83209.e: The Russian capsule lands on solid ground on a flat steppe in Kazakhstan. Just before it reaches the ground, small braking rockets fire.
83209.m: The Russian space capsule usually lands in Kazakhstan.

83210.q: What fires on the Russian space capsule just before it hits the ground?
83210.e: Just above the ground, small rockets fire. They slow the capsule down strongly once more.
83210.m: Braking rockets make the landing softer.

83211.q: What happens to the outside of the capsule when it enters the atmosphere?
83211.e: The capsule is very fast and hits the air with great force. That makes it extremely hot on the outside.
83211.m: On the way back the capsule gets very hot on the outside.

83212.q: Why can astronauts often not walk properly straight after landing?
a: Because their body has got used to floating
Because they have eaten too much
Because the ground is too hot
83212.e: After a long time in space, the body is used to being weightless. It needs a few days to get used to its weight again.
83212.m: After space, the body has to get used to walking again.

83213.q: Who picks up the astronauts after a landing in the sea?
83213.e: Rescue teams wait nearby with a ship. They bring the capsule and the astronauts on board.
83213.m: After a landing in the sea, a ship picks up the capsule.

83214.q: What is the landing of a space capsule in water called?
83214.e: When a capsule lands in the sea, it is called a splashdown. Today's American capsules land like this too.
83214.m: A landing in water is called a splashdown.

83215.q: Where do astronauts practise spacewalks on Earth?
83215.e: Under water you float almost like in space. That is why astronauts practise in spacesuits in large tanks.
83215.m: Astronauts practise floating in a water tank.

83216.q: How can astronauts briefly experience weightlessness on Earth?
a: On a parabolic flight in an aeroplane
83216.e: An aeroplane flies steeply upwards and then down in an arc. During this, everyone inside floats for about 20 seconds.
83216.m: On a parabolic flight you float for a short time.

83217.q: Which language do astronauts often learn for the space station, as well as English?
83217.e: On the space station, astronauts from the USA and from Russia work together. That is why many astronauts learn Russian.

83218.q: Why do astronauts also practise surviving in forests or in snow?
a: In case the capsule lands far away
Because they are going on holiday
83218.e: A capsule could land in a lonely place. Then the astronauts must be able to wait until help comes.
83218.m: Astronauts practise surviving in lonely places.

83219.q: Roughly how long does astronaut training take?
83219.e: Astronauts have to learn a great deal, for example about technology, medicine and space travel. That takes a few years.

83220.q: What is the European space organisation called that trains astronauts?
83220.e: ESA is short for the European Space Agency. Switzerland is a member too.

83221.q: What do astronauts practise in a replica of the space station on Earth?
a: The work and routines on board
83221.e: In a replica, all the rooms look just like those in the real space station. There the astronauts learn where everything is and how the equipment works.
83221.m: In a replica, astronauts get to know the space station.

83222.q: What are astronauts from Russia called?
83222.e: In Russia, space travellers are called cosmonauts. The word comes from cosmos, another word for space.
83222.m: Russian space travellers are called cosmonauts.

83223.q: About how old was Claude Nicollier on his first flight into space?
83223.e: Claude Nicollier was born in 1944. On his first flight in 1992 he was 47 years old.
83223.m: You can still fly into space when you are almost 50.

83224.q: Which country did the Space Shuttle that Claude Nicollier flew in come from?
83224.e: The Space Shuttle belonged to the American space agency NASA. European astronauts were allowed to fly on it.
83224.m: The Space Shuttle came from the USA.

83225.q: Where do astronauts practise using the space toilet properly?
a: On a practice toilet on Earth
In an aeroplane over the sea
Nowhere, they just try it out
83225.e: The space toilet is very different from a normal loo. That is why astronauts practise on a practice toilet before the flight.
83225.m: Astronauts practise using the space toilet on Earth.

83226.q: What do astronauts on the space station use to have a wee?
83226.e: The funnel is attached to a hose. A stream of air sucks the urine in so that nothing floats around.
83226.m: In space there is a funnel with a hose for having a wee.

83227.q: How do astronauts wash on the space station?
83227.e: Water from a shower would float around in drops. So they wash with damp wipes and no-rinse shampoo.
83227.m: On the space station you wash with damp wipes.

83228.q: What does an astronaut in a spacesuit wear on their hands?
83228.e: The gloves are a fixed part of the spacesuit. They protect the hands from cold, heat and the airless space.
83228.m: Thick gloves are part of the spacesuit.

83229.q: What do astronauts use to heat their food on the space station?
83229.e: An open fire would be far too dangerous on the space station. So the food packets are heated in a small food warmer.
83229.m: In space, food is heated in a small food warmer.

83230.q: What does an astronaut see below them during a spacewalk?
83230.e: The space station orbits not far above the Earth. So from outside you can see seas, clouds and countries.
83230.m: During a spacewalk you see the Earth below you.

83231.q: What is melted rock called while it is still deep inside the Earth?
83231.e: Under the ground, melted rock is called magma. Only at the surface is it called lava.
83231.m: Under the ground, liquid rock is called magma.

83232.q: What colour is fresh, very hot lava?
83232.e: Very hot lava glows like the embers in a fireplace. That is why it shines red to orange.
83232.m: Fresh lava glows red and orange.

83233.e: Lava is much hotter than boiling water at 100 degrees. Depending on the type, it is about 700 to 1200 degrees.
83233.m: Lava is much hotter than boiling water.

83234.q: What does lava turn into when it cools down?
83234.e: When lava cools down, it becomes solid. This makes new rock, for example dark basalt.

83235.q: What happens when a lava flow runs into the sea?
83235.e: The seawater instantly turns to steam on the hot lava. Big clouds of steam rise up.
83235.m: Lava in the sea makes the water hiss and steam.

83236.q: How fast does a lava flow often move?
a: As fast as a racing car
83236.e: Many lava flows move slowly down the mountain. But they can still destroy houses.

83237.q: On which islands in the Pacific can you often see lava flows?
83237.e: Hawaii is made of volcanoes that often pour out runny lava. It flows in long streams all the way to the sea.
83237.m: There are often lava flows on Hawaii.

a: A lump of lava flying through the air
A firework on Swiss National Day
83238.e: During an eruption, the volcano hurls scraps of lava into the air. They fall back down as volcanic bombs.
83238.m: A volcanic bomb is a flying lump of lava.

83239.q: What happens to a volcanic bomb while it is flying through the air?
a: It cools down and becomes solid
83239.e: In the air, the outside of the lump of lava cools down. That is why the bomb is already fairly solid when it lands.
83239.m: Volcanic bombs become solid in flight.

83240.q: What shape are many volcanic bombs?
83240.e: The lump of lava spins as it flies. That is why it often becomes round, or pointed at both ends like a spindle.
83240.m: Many volcanic bombs are round or spindle-shaped.

83241.q: Why must you not go near the crater during an eruption?
a: Because it is too dark there
83241.e: Volcanic bombs can be heavy and very hot. Anyone who is hit can be badly hurt.
83241.m: During an eruption it is dangerous near the crater.

83242.q: How big can volcanic bombs get?
a: Some are as big as a car
Always as small as a grain of sand
Always as big as a house
83242.e: Many volcanic bombs are the size of a fist. But there are also huge chunks as big as a car.
83242.m: Volcanic bombs can be very big.

83243.q: What are the little stones called that a volcano throws out, which are smaller than bombs?
83243.e: Lapilli is Italian and means little stones. They are about the size of peas up to nuts.
83243.m: Little stones from a volcano are called lapilli.

83244.q: How hot is a volcanic bomb when it flies out of the volcano?
a: Cool like a stone in the forest
83244.e: A volcanic bomb is a lump of lava. When it flies out of the volcano, it is red hot.

83245.q: What do you often hear when a volcano throws out bombs?
83245.e: During the eruption, big gas bubbles burst in the lava. This makes loud bangs and hurls the lava upwards.
83245.m: When volcanic bombs are thrown out, there are loud bangs.

83246.q: What shape is a volcanic crater usually?
83246.e: A crater is a round hollow. It looks like a big bowl.
83246.m: A volcanic crater looks like a bowl.

83247.q: What can form in an extinct volcanic crater?
83247.e: Rainwater collects in the crater when the volcano is no longer active. This makes a crater lake.
83247.m: A lake can form in an old crater.

83248.q: What often rises from the crater of an active volcano?
83248.e: Even without a big eruption, gases and steam come out of the crater. That is why you often see a cloud above it.
83248.m: Gases often rise from the crater.

83249.q: What is a huge, collapsed volcanic crater called?
83249.e: After a massive eruption, the volcano can collapse in on itself. This makes a huge basin, the caldera.
83249.m: A caldera is a huge collapsed crater.

83250.q: What are the small crater lakes in the Eifel in Germany called?
83250.e: There used to be volcanic eruptions in the Eifel. Today there are lakes in the round craters, which are called maars.
83250.m: The crater lakes in the Eifel are called maars.

83251.q: Does a volcano always have just one crater?
83251.e: Besides the main crater, many volcanoes have other craters on their sides. Lava can come out there too.
83251.m: A volcano can have several craters.

83252.q: What is volcanic ash made of?
83252.e: Volcanic ash is different from the ash in a fireplace. It is made of tiny bits of rock and glass.
83252.m: Volcanic ash is made of tiny bits of rock.

83253.q: Why is volcanic ash dangerous for aeroplanes?
83253.e: In the hot engines the ash melts and clogs them. That is why aeroplanes do not fly through ash clouds.
83253.m: Aeroplanes avoid clouds of volcanic ash.

83254.q: Which country did the ash cloud come from in 2010 that kept many aeroplanes on the ground in Europe?
83254.e: The volcano Eyjafjallajökull in Iceland erupted in 2010. Its ash travelled as far as central Europe, including Switzerland.
83254.m: In 2010, ash from Iceland stopped many flights in Europe.

83255.q: Which ancient Roman town was buried by volcanic ash in the year 79?
83255.e: Vesuvius in Italy erupted and covered Pompeii with ash. Today you can visit the excavated town.
83255.m: Pompeii was buried by volcanic ash.

83256.q: What should you wear when there is a lot of volcanic ash in the air?
83256.e: The fine grains of ash irritate the lungs. A mask helps you not to breathe them in.
83256.m: When there is volcanic ash in the air, a mask protects you.

83257.q: How far can the wind carry volcanic ash?
a: Only to the foot of the volcano
83257.e: Fine ash rises high into the sky. The wind can carry it thousands of kilometres.
83257.m: The wind carries volcanic ash very far.

83258.q: What colour is volcanic ash usually?
83258.e: Volcanic ash is usually grey to dark grey. It can cover cars, roads and roofs like grey snow.

83259.q: What shoots into the air at a geyser?
83259.e: Under a geyser, water is heated by hot rock. Then it shoots up as a hot fountain with steam.
83259.m: A geyser shoots hot water into the air.

83260.q: What does the Icelandic word “geysa”, which gives the geyser its name, mean?
83260.e: The Icelandic word geysa means to gush out violently. That is exactly what the hot water of a geyser does.
83260.m: The name geyser means something that gushes out violently.

83261.q: Which country in the north has lots of geysers?
83261.e: Iceland has many volcanoes and hot rock under the ground. That is why lots of geysers spout there.
83261.m: There are lots of geysers in Iceland.

83262.q: Where does the hot water of a geyser come from?
83262.e: Rainwater soaks deep into the ground. There it is heated by hot rock and shoots back up.
83262.m: The water of a geyser is heated deep inside the Earth.

83263.q: Why should you not go too close to a geyser?
83263.e: The water of a geyser can be almost boiling hot. You could scald yourself badly.

83264.q: Are there natural geysers in Switzerland?
83264.e: Geysers need hot rock close to the surface, as in Iceland. Switzerland does not have that.
83264.m: There are no natural geysers in Switzerland.

83265.q: What can you often see above a geyser, even when it is not spouting?
83265.e: The hot water in the pool is always steaming. On cold days especially, you see a lot of steam.
83265.m: Steam often rises above a geyser.

83266.q: What is special about pumice in water?
83266.e: Pumice is full of tiny air holes. That makes it so light that it floats on water.

a: It has lots of tiny holes
It is hollow inside like a balloon
83267.e: During an eruption, gas bubbles make the lava foam up. When it cools, the bubbles stay behind as holes in the stone.
83267.m: Pumice is full of tiny holes.

83268.q: What do many people use pumice for in the bathroom?
a: To rub hard skin off their feet
83268.e: Pumice is rough like sandpaper. You use it to gently rub hard skin off your feet.
83268.m: You rub hard skin off with pumice.

83269.q: What else is pumice used for?
83269.e: Because pumice is so light, it is used to make lightweight building blocks and mortar.
83269.m: Lightweight building blocks are made from pumice.

83270.e: Pumice is usually light coloured. It is often light grey, white or beige.

83271.e: Because of the many holes, the surface has sharp little edges. That is why it feels rough.

83272.q: What can float on the water after a volcanic eruption in the sea?
83272.e: Pumice is full of air holes and therefore light. After some underwater eruptions, huge rafts of pumice drift on the sea.
83272.m: After eruptions in the sea, pumice can drift on the water.

83273.q: What are some jeans washed with to make them look faded?
83273.e: The jeans were washed in the machine together with pumice stones. The rough stones rubbed off the colour.

83274.q: Which country does Mount Etna belong to?
83274.e: The island Etna stands on belongs to Italy. Italy is one of Switzerland's neighbouring countries.

83275.e: Etna is a volcano on Sicily. It is the highest active volcano in Europe.

a: Never any more, it is extinct
83276.e: Etna often has smaller and bigger eruptions. That is why scientists watch it all the time.

83277.q: What often lies on the summit of Etna in winter?
83277.e: Etna is so high that it snows at the top in winter. You can even go skiing there.
83277.m: There is often snow on Etna in winter.

83278.q: Which nuts grow especially well on Etna around Bronte?
83278.e: The little town of Bronte lies on the western slope of Etna. Famous green pistachios grow there.

83279.q: Which big city lies at the foot of Etna?
83279.e: Catania lies by the sea at the foot of Etna. In the past, lava has even flowed into the city.
83279.m: Catania lies at the foot of Etna.

83280.q: Why do many people live on Etna even though it often erupts?
a: The soil is good for fruit and vegetables
83280.e: Over time, old lava and ash turn into very fertile soil. That is why lots of fruit, vegetables and grapes for wine grow on Etna.

83281.q: Which word comes from the name of the island of Vulcano?
83281.e: The island of Vulcano gave its name to all fire-breathing mountains. That is why today we say volcano.
83281.m: The word volcano comes from the island of Vulcano.

83282.q: Which country does the island of Vulcano belong to?
83282.e: Vulcano lies in the Mediterranean north of Sicily. The island belongs to Italy.
83282.m: The island of Vulcano belongs to Italy.

83283.q: Which Roman god is the island of Vulcano named after?
83283.e: Vulcan was the Roman god of fire and blacksmiths. The Romans believed his workshop was under the island.
83283.m: Vulcan was the Roman god of fire.

83284.q: Which sea is the island of Vulcano in?
83284.e: Vulcano lies in the Mediterranean north of Sicily. The island belongs to Italy.

83285.q: What do many visitors bathe in on the island of Vulcano?
83285.e: On Vulcano there is a pool of warm mud from the volcano. Lots of people bathe in it.
83285.m: On Vulcano you can bathe in warm mud.

83286.q: What does it smell of in many places on the island of Vulcano?
83286.e: Sulphur gases rise from the ground. They smell rather unpleasantly of rotten eggs.
83286.m: On Vulcano it smells of sulphur.

83287.q: When was the last big eruption on Vulcano?
83287.e: The last eruption lasted from 1888 to 1890. Since then the volcano has been quiet, but it is closely watched.
83287.m: The volcano on Vulcano has been quiet for over 100 years.

83288.q: How do you get to the island of Vulcano?
83288.e: Vulcano is an island with no bridge to the mainland. Ferries go across from Sicily.
83288.m: You get to Vulcano by boat.

83289.e: Stromboli is a small island in the Mediterranean. It is made of an active volcano.

83290.q: Because of its many small eruptions, what else is Stromboli called?
83290.e: Stromboli often spits out glowing lava at night. Sailors saw it from far away like a light.
83290.m: Stromboli is also called the Lighthouse of the Mediterranean.

83291.q: How often does Stromboli have small eruptions?
a: Very often, usually several times an hour
Never any more, it is extinct
83291.e: Stromboli has been active almost all the time for a very long time. There are usually small eruptions several times an hour.
83291.m: Stromboli erupts a little very often.

83292.q: Do people live on the island of Stromboli?
83292.e: On Stromboli there are small villages by the sea. A few hundred people live there.
83292.m: People live on the volcanic island of Stromboli.

83293.q: Where does the glowing lava on the island of Stromboli usually slide?
83293.e: On one side of Stromboli there is a steep slope. There the lava rolls down into the sea, far away from the villages.
83293.m: On Stromboli, the lava slides into the sea.

83294.q: Roughly how high does Stromboli rise above the sea?
83294.e: The summit of Stromboli is about 920 metres above the sea. But most of the volcano is under water.

83295.q: When can you see Stromboli's glowing eruptions best?
83295.e: In the dark, the glowing lava shines brightly. During the day you mostly see smoke.
83295.m: Stromboli glows most beautifully at night.

83296.q: Which volcano gives its name to a type of eruption with small, regular explosions?
83296.e: Small, regular eruptions in which scraps of lava fly up are called Strombolian. They are named after Stromboli.
83296.m: Strombolian eruptions are named after Stromboli.

83297.q: Where should you go first at school during an earthquake?
83297.e: Under a sturdy table you are protected from things falling down. You practise this in an earthquake drill.
83297.m: In an earthquake, get under the table.

83298.q: What should you do under the table during an earthquake?
a: Protect your head and hold on
Cover your eyes and go to sleep
83298.e: You protect your head with one arm and hold on to the table leg with the other hand. That way the table does not slide away.
83298.m: Under the table, protect your head and hold on.

83299.q: What should you stay away from during an earthquake?
83299.e: Window panes can break during the quake. The splinters of glass are dangerous.
83299.m: In an earthquake, stay away from windows.

83300.q: What should you not use when leaving the building after an earthquake?
83300.e: The lift can get stuck because of a power cut. That is why you go out calmly by the stairs.
83300.m: After an earthquake, use the stairs, not the lift.

83301.q: Where are you safest outdoors during an earthquake?
a: Right next to a house wall
83301.e: In an open space nothing can fall on you. Walls, trees and power lines can fall over.
83301.m: Outdoors, an open space is safest during an earthquake.

83302.q: Why do you practise at school what to do in an earthquake?
a: So you do the right thing in an emergency
So you learn to count tables
83302.e: In a real earthquake you get a fright. If you have practised beforehand, you know straight away what to do.
83302.m: If you practise, you know what to do in an emergency.

83303.q: What should you do if you are in bed during an earthquake?
a: Stay lying down and protect your head with the pillow
83303.e: Walking around in the dark is dangerous. In bed, the pillow protects your head from things falling down.
83303.m: In bed during a quake, protect your head with the pillow.

83304.q: In which country do schoolchildren practise for earthquakes especially often?
83304.e: Japan has a great many earthquakes. That is why all children there regularly practise how to protect themselves.
83304.m: In Japan, children often practise for earthquakes.

83305.q: What should you do at the assembly point outside after an earthquake?
a: Go back into the school building
Look for a hiding place on your own
83305.e: At the assembly point the teacher counts whether all the children are there. That way you know nobody is missing.
83305.m: At the assembly point, wait until everyone is there.

83306.e: A seismograph senses how strongly the ground is shaking. That way earthquakes can be measured.

83307.q: What does a seismograph draw during an earthquake?
83307.e: When the ground is calm, the line is almost straight. During an earthquake it swings strongly back and forth.
83307.m: During a quake, a seismograph draws a zigzag line.

83308.q: What do you feel during an earthquake?
83308.e: In an earthquake the Earth moves. You feel the ground trembling and shaking.
83308.m: In an earthquake the ground shakes.

83309.q: What does a very big spike on a seismogram mean?
83309.e: The more strongly the ground shakes, the bigger the swings. So big spikes show a strong quake.
83309.m: Big spikes mean a strong earthquake.

83310.q: Which organisation in Switzerland watches earthquakes with lots of seismographs?
83310.e: The Swiss Seismological Service is part of ETH Zurich. It has set up measuring instruments all over the country.
83310.m: The Swiss Seismological Service measures earthquakes in Switzerland.

83311.q: Can seismographs also measure earthquakes that you cannot feel yourself?
83311.e: Seismographs are very sensitive. They also measure very weak earthquakes that nobody notices.
83311.m: Seismographs sense even very weak earthquakes.

83312.q: In which country was an earthquake detector with dragons built almost 2000 years ago?
83312.e: In the year 132, the scholar Zhang Heng built a device with dragons' heads. During a quake, a ball fell into the mouth of a toad.
83312.m: An earthquake detector was built in China long ago.

83313.q: Roughly how many earthquakes are measured in Switzerland each year?
83313.e: The Swiss Seismological Service measures around 1000 to 1500 earthquakes every year. Most of them are so weak that you cannot feel them.
83313.m: There are lots of small earthquakes in Switzerland every year.

83314.q: What heats up the water of a hot spring?
a: The heat deep inside the Earth
83314.e: The deeper you go into the Earth, the warmer it gets. The water flows through warm rock deep down and comes back up warm.
83314.m: The Earth's heat warms hot springs.

83315.q: In which town in the canton of Aargau did the Romans already bathe in warm spring water?
83315.e: The town of Baden has hot springs that the Romans already knew. The town's name means “baths” in German.
83315.m: The Romans already bathed in warm water in Baden.

83316.q: Which place in Valais is known for its many hot springs?
83316.e: In Leukerbad, lots of hot springs bubble out of the ground. There are big thermal baths there.
83316.m: Leukerbad in Valais has many hot springs.

83317.q: Which animals in Japan like to bathe in hot springs in winter?
83317.e: Snow monkeys live in the mountains of Japan. In winter they warm up in hot springs.
83317.m: In Japan, monkeys bathe in hot springs.

83318.q: What is a bath with warm water from the earth called?
83318.e: Thermal means warm. In a thermal bath you bathe in naturally warm spring water.
83318.m: In a thermal bath you bathe in warm spring water.

83319.q: Why do many people like bathing outdoors at a thermal bath even in winter?
83319.e: In a thermal bath, warm water comes out of the earth. That is why you can bathe outdoors in warm water even when it snows.
83319.m: In a thermal bath the water is warm even in winter.

83320.q: What is often dissolved in the water of hot springs?
83320.e: The water flows through the rock for a long time. On the way it dissolves minerals such as lime or sulphur.
83320.m: Hot spring water often contains minerals.

83321.q: Why do hot springs steam especially strongly in winter?
83321.e: The warm water gives off vapour. In cold air you can see this vapour especially well as mist.
83321.m: In cold air you can see the steam of hot springs well.

83322.q: What do volcanologists wear when they go close to a lava flow?
83322.e: A lava flow gives off great heat. A silvery suit reflects the heat and protects the scientists.
83322.m: Volcanologists protect themselves with a heat protection suit.

83323.q: What happens to trees that a lava flow reaches?
83323.e: Lava is so hot that wood catches fire at once. That is why trees in the path of a lava flow burn down.

83324.q: What can lie deep down in the crater of an active volcano?
83324.e: In some volcanoes, the lava sits in the crater like in a pot. This is called a lava lake.
83324.m: There can be a lake of lava in the crater.

83325.q: Why do people not climb down into the crater of an active volcano?
a: Because of poisonous gases and heat
Because it is too cold there
Because the path is too short
83325.e: Poisonous gases collect in the crater, and an eruption can suddenly happen. That is extremely dangerous.
83325.m: It is dangerous in the crater of an active volcano.

83326.e: Etna is over 3000 metres high. Its height changes a little because new rock is added during eruptions.

83327.q: What happens at a geyser between two eruptions?
a: It fills up with water again
83327.e: After the eruption, water flows back into the vent and is heated again. When it is hot enough, the geyser spouts again.
83327.m: A geyser fills up again between eruptions.

83328.q: What is a hot spring for bathing called in Japan?
83328.e: There are thousands of hot springs in Japan. A bath in one is called an onsen and is very popular.
83328.m: A hot spring in Japan is called an onsen.

83329.q: What happens to the sky when there is a lot of volcanic ash in the air?
83329.e: A thick ash cloud blocks the sunlight. Then it can get almost dark in the middle of the day.
83329.m: Lots of volcanic ash makes the sky dark.

83330.q: What is a candle usually made of?
83330.e: Candles are usually made of wax. The wax is the candle's fuel.
83330.m: A candle is usually made of wax.

83331.q: What material is a candle's wick usually made of?
83331.e: The wick is usually made of plaited cotton threads. They soak up the liquid wax well.
83331.m: A candle wick is usually made of cotton.

83332.q: What happens to the wax close to a candle's flame?
83332.e: The heat of the flame melts the wax. The liquid wax rises up the wick and burns there.
83332.m: The heat of the flame makes the wax liquid.

83333.q: Which animals provide wax for candles?
83333.e: Bees build their honeycombs from wax. Candles can be made from this beeswax.

83334.q: Why should you never put a candle right next to a curtain?
83334.e: Fabric burns easily. If the curtain moves towards the flame, a fire can start.
83334.m: Candles need to be kept away from anything that can burn.

83335.q: What do you do with a burning candle before leaving the room?
a: You put it by the window
83335.e: A candle must never burn without someone watching. Anyone who goes out blows it out first.
83335.m: Never leave a burning candle alone.

83336.q: What is the best thing to stand a candle on?
83336.e: A sturdy candle holder does not burn and does not tip over so easily. Cushions, paper and blankets can catch fire.
83336.m: A candle belongs on a sturdy holder that does not burn.

83337.q: What colour is the bottom part of a candle flame?
83337.e: Right at the bottom, the flame gets a lot of air and burns bluish. Further up it glows yellow.
83337.m: At the bottom, a candle flame is blue.

83338.q: Which way does a candle flame point?
83338.e: Hot air is lighter than cold air and rises. That is why the flame points upwards.
83338.m: A flame points upwards because hot air rises.

83340.q: Which gas from the air does a flame need?
83340.e: Fire needs oxygen to burn. Oxygen is part of the air.
83340.m: A flame needs oxygen from the air.

83341.q: What is the picture of the three things a fire needs called?
83341.e: Fire needs something that burns, air and enough heat. If one of them is missing, the fire goes out.
83341.m: The fire triangle shows what a fire needs to burn.

83342.q: What is a tiny glowing bit that jumps out of a fire called?
83342.e: Glowing bits can fly out of a fire. Sparks like these can set other things alight.
83342.m: A spark is a tiny glowing bit.

83343.q: What do you call a big fire that has got out of control?
83343.e: A blaze is a fire that spreads when nobody wants it to. It can destroy houses and forests.
83343.m: A fire out of control is called a blaze.

83344.q: What usually happens if you blow hard on a candle flame?
83344.e: The puff of air blows the hot gases away and cools the flame. Then it goes out.
83344.m: Blowing hard puts out a candle flame.

83345.e: A campfire is made outside at a safe fireplace. You can sit by it and roast sausages.
83345.m: A campfire burns outdoors at a fireplace.

83347.q: What is the stick of a match usually made of?
83347.e: The stick is a thin piece of wood. It burns once the head has caught fire.
83347.m: A match usually has a wooden stick.

83348.q: What is the thick part at the end of a match called?
83348.e: At the end is the match head. It contains substances that catch fire when rubbed.
83348.m: The head of a match catches fire when rubbed.

83349.q: Where does a safety match light?
a: On the striking surface of the box
83349.e: Safety matches only light when you strike them on the striking surface of the box. That is why they are called safety matches.
83349.m: A safety match lights on the striking surface of the box.

83350.q: Which substance is in the striking surface of a matchbox?
83350.e: The striking surface contains red phosphorus. Striking produces so much heat that the match head catches fire.
83350.m: The striking surface contains red phosphorus.

83351.q: In which country was the safety match invented?
83351.e: The safety match was invented in Sweden around 1844. That is why they are sometimes called Swedish matches.
83351.m: The safety match comes from Sweden.

83352.q: When may small children use matches?
83352.e: Accidents happen quickly with fire. That is why children only practise lighting matches together with adults.
83352.m: Children only light matches with adults.

83353.q: Apart from a match, what can you use to light a candle?
83353.e: A lighter makes a small flame. A torch only makes light, not fire.
83353.m: A lighter can also light a candle.

83354.q: What do you often smell first when something is burning somewhere?
83354.e: When something burns, it makes smoke with a sharp smell. You often smell it before you see the fire.
83354.m: A burning smell can be the first sign of a fire.

83355.q: Why should you crawl along the floor in a smoke-filled room?
a: There is less smoke down low
83355.e: In a fire, the air near the floor stays clean for longer. There you can breathe and see better.
83355.m: In smoke, crawl along the floor because the air is better there.

83356.q: What is often the most dangerous thing in a fire in a flat?
83356.e: Smoke is poisonous and spreads very fast. Just a few breaths can make you pass out.
83356.m: Smoke from a fire is very dangerous because it is poisonous.

83357.e: Smoke contains hot gases and very fine particles. The particles make the smoke visible.
83357.m: Smoke is made of gases and tiny particles.

83358.q: What does smoke coming from a chimney on the roof show?
a: A fire is burning in the stove
It is raining in the house
83358.e: When wood burns in the stove, the smoke goes out through the chimney. That is why you see it on the roof.
83358.m: Smoke from the chimney shows that a fire is burning in the stove.

83359.q: What does smoke often do to your eyes?
83359.e: The particles and gases in smoke irritate the eyes. That is why they sting and water.

83360.q: Complete the saying: ‘There's no smoke without ...’
83360.e: Smoke almost always comes from a fire. The saying means that every rumour has a reason behind it.
83360.m: Where there is smoke, there is usually fire.

83361.q: What do you do if there is smoke in the stairwell while you are in the flat?
a: Keep the door shut and call for help
83361.e: You can suffocate in a smoke-filled stairwell. The closed door keeps the smoke out until the fire brigade arrives.
83361.m: If there is smoke in the stairwell, stay behind the closed door.

83362.q: What rises above a sooty candle?
a: A thin black thread of smoke
83362.e: If a candle burns unsteadily, for example because the wick is too long, soot rises as a dark thread. Then you trim the wick.
83362.m: A sooty candle often has a wick that is too long.

83363.q: What is soot mainly made of?
83363.e: Soot is mainly made of tiny particles of carbon. They are left over when something does not burn completely.

83364.q: When is a lot of soot produced?
a: When something burns with too little air
83364.e: If there is not enough air, the fuel does not burn completely. Then black particles are left over.
83364.m: Too little air produces a lot of soot.

83365.q: Why does a candle flame glow yellow?
83365.e: Tiny soot particles form in the flame. They get very hot and glow yellow.
83365.m: Glowing soot particles make the candle flame yellow.

83366.q: What appears if you hold a cold spoon in a candle flame for a moment?
83366.e: The flame cools down on the cold spoon. The soot settles as a black spot.
83366.m: A cold spoon in the flame turns black from soot.

83367.q: Who cleans the soot out of chimneys?
83367.e: The chimney sweep cleans chimneys and stoves. That way the soot cannot catch fire and the smoke can escape properly.
83367.m: The chimney sweep cleans the soot out of the chimney.

83368.q: Which job is thought to bring good luck?
83368.e: In the past, the chimney sweep protected houses from fires. That is why chimney sweeps are still thought to bring good luck today.
83368.m: The chimney sweep is thought to bring good luck.

83369.q: What was black ink for writing made from in the past?
83369.e: Soot was mixed with water and glue. This made black ink for writing and painting.
83369.m: Black ink used to be made from soot.

83370.q: Where does wood ash go once it has cooled down completely?
83370.e: Completely cold ash with no embers may go in the rubbish. It does not belong in the recycling collections.
83370.m: Cooled ash belongs in the rubbish.

83371.q: What colour is wood ash usually?
83371.e: Wood ash is usually light grey to grey. It is a soft powder.

83372.q: Why should ash not be emptied into the rubbish bag straight away?
a: There may still be embers in it
83372.e: Embers can stay hidden in ash for a long time. In the rubbish bag they could start a fire.
83372.m: Embers can stay hidden in ash for a long time.

83373.q: What is the safest thing to keep fresh ash in?
a: A metal bucket with a lid
83373.e: Metal does not burn. The lid keeps air away, so leftover embers cannot set anything alight.
83373.m: Fresh ash goes in a metal bucket with a lid.

83374.q: How heavy is the ash compared with the wood before?
83374.e: When it burns, almost all of the wood turns into gases. Only a small amount is left behind as ash.
83374.m: Ash is much lighter than the wood was.

83375.q: What did people make from wood ash and fat in the past?
83375.e: An alkali was made from wood ash and water. Boiled with fat, it turned into soap.
83375.m: In the past, soap was made from ash and fat.

83376.q: What do some gardeners use wood ash for?
83376.e: Wood ash contains substances that plants need. That is why some people sprinkle small amounts of it in the garden.
83376.m: Wood ash can be a fertiliser for plants.

83377.q: What are the still glowing remains of a fire called?
83377.e: Embers glow red and are very hot, even without a flame. Never touch them.
83377.m: Embers are the glowing remains of a fire.

83378.q: What colour are fire extinguishers usually?
83378.e: Fire extinguishers are usually red. That way you can find them quickly in an emergency.

83379.q: What is a fire extinguisher for?
83379.e: With a fire extinguisher you can fight a small fire. Big fires are put out by the fire brigade.
83379.m: A fire extinguisher puts out small fires.

83380.q: What pushes the extinguishing agent out of a fire extinguisher?
83380.e: Inside the fire extinguisher is a gas under pressure. When you squeeze the handle, it forces the extinguishing agent through the hose.
83380.m: A gas under pressure drives the agent out of the fire extinguisher.

83381.q: What comes out of a foam extinguisher?
83381.e: A foam extinguisher sprays foam. The foam covers what is burning and cools it.
83381.m: A foam extinguisher puts out fires with foam.

83382.q: What do you have to pull out before a fire extinguisher will work?
83382.e: A pin locks the handle. Only when it has been pulled out can you put out the fire.
83382.m: With a fire extinguisher, you first pull out the safety pin.

83383.q: Where do you aim the jet of a fire extinguisher?
a: At the base of the burning object
Into the air above the fire
83383.e: You put out the fire where it is really burning, at the bottom where it starts. Spraying into the smoke does little good.
83383.m: Aim at the bottom of the burning object, not into the smoke.

83384.q: Where is a fire extinguisher usually kept in a school building?
a: On the wall where it is easy to see
83384.e: In an emergency you have to find the fire extinguisher quickly. That is why it hangs where it is easy to see in the corridor, often with a sign.
83384.m: Fire extinguishers hang on the wall where they are easy to see.

83385.q: Who should use a fire extinguisher?
83385.e: A fire extinguisher is heavy and must be used properly. Children fetch help and get themselves to safety.
83385.m: Fire extinguishers are used by adults.

83386.q: About how long can a small fire extinguisher spray for?
83386.e: A small hand-held fire extinguisher is often empty after only about 10 to 20 seconds. That is why you have to aim carefully.
83386.m: A small fire extinguisher is empty after just a few seconds.

83387.q: What is a fire blanket for?
83387.e: You cover a small fire with a fire blanket. This smothers it.
83387.m: A fire blanket smothers small fires.

83388.q: How does a fire blanket put out a fire?
a: It takes the air away from the fire
83388.e: Under the blanket no fresh air can reach the fire. Without air it goes out.
83388.m: The fire blanket takes away the fire's air.

83389.q: In which room is a fire blanket often kept?
83389.e: The kitchen is where cooking and frying happen. Oil in a pan can easily catch fire there.
83389.m: A fire blanket often hangs in the kitchen.

83390.q: What can you cover a burning pan with if there is no fire blanket?
83390.e: A metal lid does not burn and closes the pan tightly. Without air, the fire goes out.
83390.m: A lid that fits can put out a burning pan.

83391.q: What is a fire blanket often made of?
83391.e: Fire blankets are made of a fabric that does not burn, often glass fibre. Paper, plastic and silk would catch fire.
83391.m: A fire blanket is made of a fabric that does not burn.

83392.q: How do you get a fire blanket out of its case quickly?
83392.e: Two tapes hang from the case. If you pull them hard, the blanket falls out.
83392.m: Pull the tapes to get the fire blanket out.

83393.q: Why do you hold the fire blanket so that your hands are behind it?
83393.e: The blanket is like a shield in front of the flames. That way you don't burn your hands.
83393.m: Behind the fire blanket, your hands are protected.

83394.q: What do you do with the fire blanket after covering the pan?
a: You pull it off at once
83394.e: It can stay hot under the blanket for a long time. If you lift it off too soon, the fire can flare up again.
83394.m: Leave the fire blanket in place until everything has cooled down.

83395.q: What does a smoke alarm do when it detects smoke?
83395.e: A smoke alarm makes a very loud warning sound. That way everyone is warned, even while asleep.
83395.m: A smoke alarm warns with a loud beep.

83396.q: Where is a smoke alarm fitted?
83396.e: The smoke alarm detects smoke where it gathers first in a room. That way it warns as early as possible.
83396.m: A smoke alarm belongs on the ceiling.

83397.q: What does a smoke alarm usually need in order to work?
83397.e: Most smoke alarms have a battery. That way they work even in a power cut.
83397.m: A smoke alarm usually needs a battery.

83398.q: How do you check whether a smoke alarm works?
83398.e: Every smoke alarm has a test button. When you press it, the warning sound must go off.
83398.m: You check a smoke alarm with the test button.

83399.q: Why is a smoke alarm in the bedroom especially important?
a: You can't smell smoke while asleep
Cooking is done in the bedroom
83399.e: Sleeping people do not notice smoke and do not wake up from it. The loud sound of the smoke alarm wakes them.
83399.m: A smoke alarm wakes us because we can't smell smoke while asleep.

83400.q: What do you do if the smoke alarm goes off and there is a fire?
83400.e: Smoke spreads very fast. That is why you go out at once and get help outside.
83400.m: When the smoke alarm goes off, leave the flat at once.

83401.q: What does a short beep from a smoke alarm every few minutes often mean?
a: There is a fire in the cellar
83401.e: Many smoke alarms give a short beep when the battery gets weak. Then it needs changing soon.
83401.m: A short beep often means a weak battery.

83402.q: How often should you check a smoke alarm?
a: Only when there is a fire
83402.e: Only a working smoke alarm can warn you. That is why you check it regularly with the test button.

83403.q: What shape are the hazard symbols on chemicals?
83403.e: The hazard symbols are diamonds, that is squares standing on one corner. Inside is a black picture.

83404.q: What colour is the border of a hazard symbol?
83404.e: Hazard symbols have a red border and a white background. The black picture shows the danger.
83404.m: Hazard symbols have a red border.

83405.q: What does the hazard symbol with a flame mean?
83405.e: The flame shows that this substance can catch fire easily. Keep it away from heat and flames.
83405.m: The flame symbol warns of highly flammable substances.

83406.q: What does the hazard symbol with a skull and crossbones mean?
83406.e: The skull and crossbones warns of very poisonous substances. Even small amounts can be deadly.
83406.m: The skull and crossbones warns of poison.

83407.q: What does the hazard symbol with a dead tree and a fish mean?
83407.e: This substance harms animals and plants, especially in water. It must not go down the drain.
83407.m: The tree and fish warn of danger to the environment.

83408.q: What does the hazard symbol with an exploding bomb mean?
83408.e: The exploding bomb warns of substances that can explode. You have to be very careful with them.
83408.m: The bomb warns of explosive substances.

83409.q: What does the hazard symbol with a flame over a circle mean?
83409.e: Such substances give off oxygen. They make a fire stronger, even if they do not burn themselves.
83409.m: The flame over a circle warns of oxidising substances.

83410.q: On which things at home do you often find hazard symbols?
83410.e: Many cleaning products contain dangerous substances. That is why they carry hazard symbols.
83410.m: Many cleaning products carry hazard symbols.

83411.q: What does the hazard symbol with drops attacking a hand mean?
83411.e: Corrosive substances can injure skin and eyes. That is why the symbol shows a hand being attacked.
83411.m: The symbol with the hand warns of corrosive substances.

83412.q: What is the first thing you do in a fire?
83412.e: The rule is: raise the alarm, rescue, put out. First you call for help, then you get people to safety.
83412.m: In a fire, first raise the alarm, then rescue, then put it out.

83413.q: What should you do if your own clothes are on fire?
83413.e: Running gives the fire more air. If you lie down and roll, you smother the flames.
83413.m: If your clothes are on fire, lie down and roll.

83414.q: What do you use to get out of a building on fire?
83414.e: The lift can get stuck in a fire. That is why you always take the stairs.
83414.m: In a fire, take the stairs, never the lift.

83415.q: Why do you close the door when leaving a room on fire?
a: It holds back smoke and fire
83415.e: A closed door slows down smoke and flames. That way the escape route stays clear for longer.
83415.m: A closed door slows down smoke and fire.

83416.q: What colour are emergency exit signs?
83416.e: Emergency exits and escape routes are marked with green signs. They show a white figure running to a door.

83417.q: What should you not do when escaping from a fire?
83417.e: Looking for things wastes precious time. People are more important than things.
83417.m: In a fire, save yourself, not your toys.

83418.q: Where does everyone meet during a fire drill at school?
83418.e: After leaving the school building, everyone goes to the assembly point. There the teacher can see whether everyone is there.
83418.m: After a fire alarm, everyone meets at the assembly point.

83419.q: Who comes in red vehicles to put out fires?
83419.e: The fire brigade drives red vehicles with blue lights. It puts out fires and rescues people.
83419.m: The fire brigade puts out fires and rescues people.

83420.q: What is barbecue charcoal made from?
83420.e: Barbecue charcoal is charcoal made from wood. Wood is heated with little air until it turns into charcoal.
83420.m: Barbecue charcoal is made from wood.

83421.q: What is the job of people who make charcoal called?
83421.e: Charcoal burners turn wood into charcoal in a big pile. In the Entlebuch in the canton of Lucerne there are still charcoal burners today.

83422.q: What is the big pile of wood in which charcoal burners make charcoal called?
83422.e: In a charcoal kiln, wood is covered with earth. It smoulders there for days with little air and turns into charcoal.
83422.m: In a charcoal kiln, wood turns into charcoal.

83423.q: What must you never pour onto glowing barbecue charcoal?
83423.e: Methylated spirits and petrol evaporate and catch fire explosively. A dangerous jet of flame shoots up.
83423.m: Never pour methylated spirits or petrol onto glowing charcoal.

83424.q: How can you tell that the barbecue charcoal is ready for grilling?
a: It is covered in grey ash
83424.e: When the charcoal is glowing right through, a grey layer lies on it. Then it gives off even heat.
83424.m: Grey charcoal is ready for grilling.

83425.q: Why must you never use a charcoal barbecue in a closed room?
a: The charcoal goes out at once
83425.e: Glowing charcoal produces carbon monoxide. This gas is poisonous and you cannot smell it.
83425.m: A charcoal barbecue belongs outdoors only.

83426.q: What do you use to light barbecue charcoal safely?
83426.e: Firelighters burn slowly and evenly. That way the charcoal lights without a jet of flame.

83427.q: What do you use to turn sausages on a hot barbecue?
83427.e: Barbecue tongs are long and made of metal. That way your fingers stay well away from the embers.

83428.q: Which plant gave the inventor the idea for Velcro?
83428.e: The burrs of the burdock have tiny hooks. With them they get caught in fur and clothes.
83428.m: Burdock was the model for Velcro.

83429.e: On one side there are lots of tiny hooks, on the other soft loops. When you press them together, they hook into each other.
83429.m: With Velcro, hooks hold in loops.

83430.q: What sound does Velcro make when you open it?
83430.e: When you pull it open, lots of hooks come loose at the same time. That makes a ripping sound.
83430.m: Velcro makes a ripping sound when opened.

83431.q: On which shoes do you often find Velcro fastenings?
83431.e: Children can quickly fasten shoes with Velcro by themselves. They do not have to tie laces.
83431.m: With Velcro, shoes are fastened quickly.

83432.q: What is on the rough side of a Velcro fastening?
83432.e: On the rough side there are lots of tiny hooks. They grip into the soft loops on the other side.

83433.q: What often builds up in a Velcro fastening over time?
83433.e: The hooks catch fluff and hair. Then the fastening holds less well.
83433.m: Fluff often builds up in the hooks.

83434.q: When does a Velcro fastening stay closed?
a: When you press both sides together
83434.e: The fastening only holds once the hooks grip the loops. That is why you press the two parts firmly together.
83434.m: Velcro holds when you press both parts together.

83435.q: Where do astronauts use Velcro too?
83435.e: In weightlessness, things float away. With Velcro strips you can fix objects to the walls.
83435.m: On the space station, Velcro strips hold things in place.

83436.q: Which country did George de Mestral come from?
83436.e: George de Mestral was born in 1907 in western Switzerland. He lived and worked in Switzerland.

83437.q: Which plant gave George de Mestral the idea for Velcro?
83437.e: After a walk, lots of burdock burrs were stuck to his clothes and his dog’s fur. Under the microscope he saw tiny hooks.
83437.m: Burdock was the model for Velcro.

83438.q: Which animal had burrs in its fur after George de Mestral’s outing?
83438.e: After a hunting trip, burrs were stuck in his dog’s fur. That made him curious.
83438.m: Burrs in his dog’s fur gave George de Mestral the idea.

83439.q: What did George de Mestral use to look closely at the burrs?
83439.e: Under the microscope he saw the tiny, springy hooks of the burrs. That is how he understood why they stick.
83439.m: Under the microscope, de Mestral discovered the burrs’ hooks.

83440.q: What was George de Mestral’s job?
83440.e: George de Mestral studied engineering at a university. After that he worked as an engineer.
83440.m: George de Mestral was an engineer.

83441.q: How does a Velcro fastening hold together?
83441.e: One side has lots of small hooks, the other soft loops. When you press them together, they hook into each other.

83442.q: Roughly how long did George de Mestral work on Velcro before he applied for the patent?
83442.e: He had the idea in 1941 after an outing with his dog. He only applied for the patent in 1951, because for a long time the hooks did not hold well.
83442.m: A good invention often takes many years of work.

83443.q: In which part of Switzerland was George de Mestral born?
83443.e: He was born in 1907 in Saint-Saphorin-sur-Morges in the canton of Vaud. That is in French-speaking western Switzerland.
83443.m: George de Mestral was born in western Switzerland.

83444.q: What colour is the well-known Swiss army knife usually?
83444.e: The handle scales are usually red. They show the Swiss cross.
83444.m: The Swiss army knife is usually red.

83445.q: Which symbol is on many Swiss army knives?
83445.e: On the red handle there is an emblem with the Swiss cross. It shows where the knife comes from.
83445.m: The Swiss cross is on the pocket knife.

83446.q: Who received the first Swiss soldier’s knives in 1891?
83446.e: In 1891 the Swiss Army received its first soldier’s knife. That is where the English name Swiss Army Knife comes from.
83446.m: The pocket knife was first made for the Swiss Army.

83447.q: Who founded the well-known knife factory in Ibach?
83447.e: Karl Elsener opened a cutlery workshop in Ibach in 1884. It grew into a world-famous company.
83447.m: Karl Elsener founded the knife factory in Ibach.

83448.q: In which canton is Ibach, where pocket knives are made?
83448.e: Ibach is part of the municipality of Schwyz. Pocket knives have been made there for more than a hundred years.
83448.m: Ibach is in the canton of Schwyz.

83449.q: Why can you put a pocket knife in your trouser pocket?
83449.e: All the tools fold into the handle. That way the knife is small and the blade is protected.
83449.m: On a pocket knife, the blades fold into the handle.

83450.q: Which tool does a pocket knife often have for opening wine bottles?
83450.e: The corkscrew is a twisted spiral. You twist it into the cork and pull the cork out.
83450.m: You pull corks out of bottles with a corkscrew.

83451.q: Who was the first Swiss pocket knife made for?
83451.e: In 1891 Swiss soldiers received their first pocket knife. Later the officer’s knife with even more tools was added.
83451.m: The first Swiss pocket knife was for soldiers.

83452.q: What should children do when whittling with a pocket knife?
83452.e: If you whittle away from your body, you cannot cut yourself so easily. If the blade slips, it goes into thin air.
83452.m: Always whittle away from your body.

83453.q: What is the part you pull up and down on a zip called?
83453.e: The slider runs over the teeth. It joins them together or separates them.
83453.m: The slider opens and closes the zip.

83454.e: There are lots of small teeth on both sides. The slider presses them together so that they hook into each other.
83454.m: In a zip, small teeth interlock.

83455.q: What can happen if fabric gets caught in a zip?
83455.e: If fabric gets between the teeth, the slider cannot move on. Then you carefully pull it back.
83455.m: Fabric in a zip makes it jam.

83456.q: On which piece of clothing do you often find a long zip?
83456.e: Many jackets are closed at the front with a long zip. That is faster than with lots of buttons.

83457.q: In which country was the first forerunner of the zip invented?
83457.e: In 1893 Whitcomb Judson presented a fastener with hooks in Chicago. It was later improved into today’s zip.
83457.m: The zip has its beginnings in the USA.

83458.q: What is a zip made of?
a: Two rows of teeth and a slider
83458.e: The slider presses the teeth of the two rows into each other or separates them again. This design became established around 1913.
83458.m: In a zip, a slider joins two rows of teeth.

83459.q: What happens if a tooth of the zip is missing?
83459.e: If a tooth is missing, the teeth do not interlock properly there. The zip can burst open at that spot.
83459.m: A missing tooth can make the zip come open.

83460.q: What are the teeth of a zip often made of?
83460.e: The teeth have to be strong and small. That is why they are made of metal or plastic.
83460.m: The teeth are made of metal or plastic.

83461.q: How were letters put onto paper in old-style book printing?
83461.e: The letters were coated with ink. Then a press pushed the paper firmly onto them.
83461.m: In book printing, paper is pressed onto inked letters.

83462.q: What are the individual metal letters used in book printing called?
83462.e: Each letter was a small block of metal. Together they are called movable type.
83462.m: The letters used in book printing are called type.

83463.q: Why is the writing on a stamp back to front?
a: So it comes out the right way round on the paper
83463.e: When you stamp, the image is reversed. That is why the writing on the stamp has to be back to front. It was just the same in old-style book printing.
83463.m: The writing on a stamp is a mirror image.

83464.q: What could be made much faster thanks to book printing?
83464.e: Before that, books were laboriously copied by hand. With printing, many identical pages could be made quickly.
83464.m: Printing made books faster and cheaper to make.

83465.q: Which machine pressed the paper onto the type in book printing?
83465.e: The printing press pushed the paper evenly onto the inked type. That way every page came out clean.
83465.m: The printing press pushes the paper onto the type.

83466.q: Why could the type be used again and again in book printing?
a: It could be put together in new ways
It was carved anew each time
It was melted down after each print
The same page was always printed
83466.e: After printing, the letters were taken apart. Then they were put together into new words for the next page.
83466.m: Movable type can always be rearranged.

83467.q: Which Swiss city became an important centre of book printing early on?
83467.e: There were print shops in Basel as early as around 1470. The city became an important place for books.
83467.m: Basel was an important printing city early on.

83468.q: What was the job of the people who used to put the type together into words called?
83468.e: The typesetter put the lines together letter by letter. Only then could printing begin.
83468.m: The typesetter put the type together.

83469.q: In which city did Johannes Gutenberg live and print?
83469.e: Johannes Gutenberg was born in Mainz and had his workshop there. Mainz is on the Rhine.

83470.q: Which famous book did Johannes Gutenberg print?
83470.e: The Gutenberg Bible was made around 1454. It is one of the first large printed books in Europe.

83471.q: In which century did Johannes Gutenberg live?
83471.e: Gutenberg lived from about 1400 to 1468. That is the 15th century.
83471.m: Johannes Gutenberg lived in the 15th century.

83472.q: What did Johannes Gutenberg invent around 1450?
83472.e: Gutenberg cast individual letters from metal that could be put together again and again. That way books could be made much faster.
83472.m: Gutenberg invented printing with movable type.

83473.q: What can you see at the Gutenberg Museum in Mainz?
83473.e: At the Gutenberg Museum in Mainz you can see old printing presses and Gutenberg Bibles.
83473.m: There is a Gutenberg Museum in Mainz.

83474.q: In which country is Johannes Gutenberg’s home town today?
83474.e: Mainz is on the Rhine in Germany. There is also a monument to Gutenberg there.
83474.m: Gutenberg’s home town is in Germany today.

83475.q: Apart from books, what else did Johannes Gutenberg print?
83475.e: Gutenberg also printed small works such as a calendar for the year 1455. Newspapers, postage stamps and banknotes were only printed in Europe much later.

83476.q: What does a magnifying glass do with small things?
83476.e: Through a magnifying glass, a small object looks much bigger. That way you can make out details.
83476.m: A magnifying glass makes small things bigger.

83477.q: Why must you not leave a magnifying glass lying in the sun?
83477.e: The magnifying glass focuses sunlight onto a small spot. It can get so hot there that paper catches fire.
83477.m: A magnifying glass in the sun can start a fire.

83478.q: What can you observe well with a magnifying glass?
83478.e: A magnifying glass helps with small things that are close. For distant things you need a telescope.
83478.m: Use a magnifying glass to observe small things up close.

83479.q: Which famous detective is often shown with a magnifying glass?
83479.e: Sherlock Holmes searches for clues with a magnifying glass. That is why the magnifying glass is a symbol for detectives.
83479.m: Sherlock Holmes searches for clues with a magnifying glass.

83480.q: What is another name for a magnifier?
83480.e: A magnifier enlarges what you look at through it. That is why it is also called a magnifying glass.
83480.m: A magnifier is also called a magnifying glass.

83481.q: What happens if you hold the magnifying glass too far from the object?
83481.e: A magnifying glass only shows a sharp image at a certain distance. If it is too far away, the image becomes fuzzy.
83481.m: A magnifying glass needs the right distance for a sharp image.

83482.q: What can you use in an emergency to magnify something like a magnifying glass?
83482.e: A round drop of water works like a small lens. Letters underneath it look bigger.
83482.m: A drop of water can work like a magnifying glass.

83483.e: The lenses bend the light so that a sharp image forms in the eye.

83484.q: What are the parts of a pair of glasses that rest over the ears called?
83484.e: The arms hold the glasses in place behind the ears. That way they do not slip off your nose.
83484.m: The arms hold the glasses on your ears.

83485.q: Where do people in Switzerland usually buy glasses?
83485.e: The optician measures your eyes and fits the glasses. They also grind the right lenses.
83485.m: You get glasses from the optician.

83486.q: In which country were glasses invented more than 700 years ago?
83486.e: The first glasses were made around 1285 in northern Italy. They were reading glasses.

83487.q: Which glasses protect your eyes from strong sun?
83487.e: Good sunglasses block harmful UV light. That is especially important in the mountains and in snow.
83487.m: Sunglasses protect your eyes from strong sun.

83488.q: What do you need to see well when swimming under water?
83488.e: Diving goggles keep the water away from your eyes. With air in front of your eyes, you see clearly under water.
83488.m: With diving goggles you see well under water.

83489.q: What do you call people who cannot see clearly into the distance?
83489.e: Short-sighted people see close things well, but distant things are blurred. Glasses help them.
83489.m: Short-sighted people see distant things blurred.

83490.q: What is the best thing to clean glasses lenses with?
83490.e: Soft cloths clean the lenses without scratching them. Rough things would make scratches.
83490.m: Clean glasses lenses with a soft cloth.

83491.q: What do many people wear directly on the eye instead of glasses?
83491.e: Contact lenses are small, thin lenses. You put them directly onto the eye.
83491.m: Contact lenses sit directly on the eye.

83492.e: The Swatch is a wristwatch from Switzerland. It is especially colourful.
83492.m: The Swatch is a Swiss wristwatch.

83493.q: In which year did the first Swatch come out?
83493.e: The Swatch went on sale in Zurich on 1 March 1983.
83493.m: The first Swatch came out in 1983.

83494.q: What material is the case of the classic Swatch made of?
83494.e: The classic Swatch has a plastic case. That is why it is light and cheap.
83494.m: The classic Swatch is made of plastic.

83495.q: What was different about the Swatch compared with many other Swiss watches?
83495.e: Many Swiss watches were expensive. The Swatch was cheap, so lots of people could buy one.
83495.m: The Swatch was an affordable Swiss watch.

83496.q: In which Swiss city does the Swatch company have its headquarters?
83496.e: The company has its headquarters in Biel. Biel is an important city of the watch industry.
83496.m: The Swatch company is based in Biel.

83497.q: Which businessman is regarded as the father of the Swatch?
83497.e: From 1984, Nicolas G. Hayek made the Swatch famous all over the world. That is why he is called the father of the Swatch.
83497.m: Nicolas G. Hayek is regarded as the father of the Swatch.

a: To wake children in the morning
83498.e: Cheap watches from Asia were worrying the Swiss companies. With the affordable Swatch, they could sell lots of watches again.
83498.m: The Swatch helped the Swiss watch industry out of a crisis.

83499.q: What is the Swatch especially known for?
83499.e: There are many Swatch models in every colour. Some were designed by artists.
83499.m: The Swatch is known for its bright colours.

83500.q: Which Swiss man developed a famous milk chocolate in 1875?
83500.e: Daniel Peter mixed cocoa and sugar with milk. That was very difficult at the time, because milk contains a lot of water.
83500.m: Daniel Peter developed a famous Swiss milk chocolate.

83501.q: Why was it so difficult for Daniel Peter to mix milk into chocolate?
a: Milk contains a lot of water
83501.e: Water and cocoa butter do not mix well, and the chocolate quickly went mouldy. That is why Daniel Peter experimented for many years.
83501.m: The water in milk was the big problem with milk chocolate.

83502.q: In which town on Lake Geneva did Daniel Peter work on his milk chocolate?
83502.e: Daniel Peter had his chocolate factory in Vevey on Lake Geneva. There he developed his milk chocolate.

83503.q: Which milk did Daniel Peter use for his chocolate?
a: Goat’s milk fresh from the barn
83503.e: Daniel Peter used thickened milk with only a little water left in it. That is how he succeeded with his milk chocolate in 1875.
83503.m: Daniel Peter used condensed milk for his chocolate.

83504.q: Which neighbour in Vevey helped Daniel Peter with his experiments?
83504.e: Henri Nestlé also lived in Vevey and knew a lot about milk. He helped Daniel Peter bring his chocolate to market.
83504.m: Henri Nestlé supported Daniel Peter in his experiments.

83505.q: Which beans is chocolate made from?
83505.e: Cocoa beans grow on the cocoa tree in warm countries. They are roasted and ground.
83505.m: Chocolate is made from cocoa beans.

83506.e: The milk makes the chocolate lighter. That is why milk chocolate is light brown.

83507.q: Who invented the conche in Bern, which makes chocolate melt smoothly?
83507.e: Rodolphe Lindt invented the conche in Bern in 1879. In it, the chocolate mass is stirred for a long time and so becomes smooth.
83507.m: Rodolphe Lindt made chocolate melt smoothly.

83508.q: What happens to chocolate in the sun on a hot summer’s day?
83508.e: Chocolate melts at around body temperature. In the hot sun it becomes soft and runny.

83509.q: What do you use a peeler for?
83509.e: With the peeler you peel potatoes and carrots, for example. It only takes off a thin layer.
83509.m: A peeler peels vegetables and fruit.

83511.q: What do you use the Rex peeler for?
83511.e: With the Rex you peel potatoes, carrots or apples. The movable blade only cuts off a thin layer, so little is wasted.
83511.m: The Rex is a Swiss peeler for vegetables and fruit.

83512.q: In which year was the Rex peeler registered for a patent?
83512.e: The Rex was registered in 1947. It has looked almost the same ever since.
83512.m: The Rex peeler has existed since 1947.

83513.q: What is special about the Rex peeler?
a: The blade is crosswise and movable
83513.e: On the Rex, the blade lies crosswise to the handle and can move. That way it adapts to every curve.
83513.m: The Rex has a crosswise, movable blade.

83514.q: What material is the handle of the classic Rex peeler made of?
83514.e: The classic Rex is bent from a single piece of aluminium. It is light and does not rust.
83514.m: The classic Rex is made of aluminium.

83515.q: How did Swiss Post honour the Rex peeler?
83515.e: At the end of 2003 a 15-centime stamp showing the Rex came out. It is considered a classic of Swiss design.
83515.m: The Rex got its own postage stamp.

83516.q: Which country does the Rex peeler come from?
83516.e: The Rex was invented in Switzerland in 1947 and was made in the canton of Zurich for a long time. Today it belongs to Victorinox.
83516.m: The Rex peeler is a Swiss invention.

83517.q: What is the lead of a pencil made of?
83517.e: Despite the name, there is no lead in a pencil. The lead is made of graphite mixed with clay.
83517.m: A pencil contains graphite, not lead.

83518.q: What is the casing of a pencil usually made of?
83518.e: The lead sits inside a wooden casing. The wood protects the fragile lead.
83518.m: The casing of a pencil is usually made of wood.

83519.q: What can you use to remove pencil lines?
83519.e: The rubber rubs the graphite particles off the paper. That way the line disappears.

83520.q: What do you use to make a blunt pencil sharp again?
83520.e: A sharpener has a small blade inside. It cuts the wood and lead into a cone shape.
83520.m: You sharpen a pencil with a sharpener.

83521.q: What does the letter B on a pencil mean?
a: The lead is soft and black
The lead is hard and pale
83521.e: B stands for soft leads that write dark. H stands for hard, pale leads.
83521.m: B on a pencil means a soft, dark lead.

83522.q: Which pencil company is based in Geneva?
83522.e: Caran d’Ache has been making pencils in Geneva for more than a hundred years. The name comes from the Russian word for pencil.
83522.m: Caran d’Ache makes pencils in Geneva.

a: So they do not roll off the table
83523.e: A round pencil rolls away easily. The six edges keep the pencil on the table.
83523.m: Hexagonal pencils do not roll away so easily.

83524.q: Which hardness grade is a medium pencil for school?
83524.e: HB lies between the hard H leads and the soft B leads. That is why it is often used at school.

83526.q: What is the digit sum of the number 2026?
83526.e: You add all the digits: 2 + 0 + 2 + 6 makes 10.
83526.m: The digit sum is the sum of all the digits of a number.

83527.q: A number is divisible by 3 exactly when ... ?
a: its digit sum is divisible by 3
its first digit is divisible by 3
83527.e: You can tell divisibility by 3 from the digit sum. For 471 the digit sum is 12, so 471 is also divisible by 3.
83527.m: The digit sum is a quick check for divisibility by 3.

83528.q: How does the digit sum change if you add a zero to the end of a number?
a: It becomes ten times as big
83528.e: 47 becomes 470. In both cases the digit sum is 4 + 7, so 11, because the zero adds nothing.
83528.m: Zeros do not change the digit sum of a number.

83529.q: What is the digit sum of 999?
83529.m: With nothing but nines, the digit sum is nine times the number of digits.

83530.q: What is the repeated digit sum of 98?
83530.e: The digit sum of 98 is 17, and the digit sum of 17 is 8. You keep going until only one digit is left.
83530.m: For the repeated digit sum, you keep taking the digit sum until a single-digit number is left.

83531.q: What is the smallest natural number with a digit sum of 20?
83531.e: For the smallest possible number you need as few places as possible and digits at the end as large as possible: 2 + 9 + 9 makes 20. Two places are not enough, because 9 + 9 is only 18.
83531.m: The smallest number with a given digit sum has as many nines at the end as possible.

83532.q: The alternating digit sum is used to check divisibility by which number?
83532.e: You take the digits alternately with plus and minus, starting from the end. For 3245, 5 − 4 + 2 − 3 makes zero, so 3245 is divisible by 11.
83532.m: The alternating digit sum reveals divisibility by 11.

83533.q: The number 7_2 is divisible by 9. Which digit goes in the gap?
83533.e: The digit sum 7 + ? + 2 must be divisible by 9. That works for 9 (digit 0, number 702) and for 18 (digit 9, number 792).
83533.m: You find missing digits by completing the digit sum to fit.

83534.q: What is the digit sum of the smallest five-digit number?
83534.e: The smallest five-digit number is 10000. 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 makes 1.
83534.m: The digit sum of 10, 100, 1000 and so on is always 1.

83535.q: What is the prime factorisation of 72?
83535.e: 72 = 8 · 9, so 2 · 2 · 2 · 3 · 3. In short, you write this as 2³ · 3².
83535.m: At the end of a prime factorisation, there are only prime numbers.

83536.q: What is the prime factorisation of 100?
83536.e: 100 = 4 · 25, and 4 is 2 · 2 and 25 is 5 · 5. So 100 equals 2² · 5².
83536.m: The numbers 10, 100 and 1000 are made only of the prime factors 2 and 5.

83537.q: Which number has the prime factorisation 2 · 3 · 7?
83537.m: If you multiply all the prime factors, you get the original number back.

83538.q: In how many ways can you split the number 30 into prime factors if the order does not matter?
83538.e: 30 is always 2 · 3 · 5, however you start. Every natural number greater than 1 has exactly one prime factorisation.
83538.m: Every natural number greater than 1 can be split into prime factors in only one way.

83539.q: How many prime factors (counted with repetition) does the number 64 have?
83539.m: Powers of two are made only of the prime factor 2.

83540.q: What is the highest common factor (HCF) of 12 and 18?
83540.e: 12 = 2² · 3 and 18 = 2 · 3². They share one factor 2 and one factor 3, so the HCF is 6.
83540.m: For the HCF you take the shared prime factors.

83541.q: What is the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 4 and 6?
83541.e: 4 = 2² and 6 = 2 · 3. The LCM needs 2² and 3, so 4 · 3, which makes 12.
83541.m: For the LCM you take each prime factor in its highest power.

83542.q: What is the prime factorisation of 126?
83542.m: You keep dividing by prime numbers until only 1 is left.

83543.q: Why is the prime factorisation of large numbers important for encryption on the internet?
a: Large numbers are very hard to factorise
Large numbers have no prime factors
83543.e: Methods such as RSA rely on the fact that you can easily multiply two huge prime numbers, but can hardly split the product again.
83543.m: Factorising huge numbers is so hard that it can protect data.

83544.q: Who was Eratosthenes, after whom the famous prime number sieve is named?
a: A Greek scholar of ancient times
83544.e: Eratosthenes of Cyrene lived in the 3rd century BC and ran the famous Library of Alexandria.
83544.m: The Sieve of Eratosthenes comes from ancient Greece.

83545.q: In the Sieve of Eratosthenes, which numbers do you cross out after circling the 2?
83545.e: Every multiple of 2, so 4, 6, 8 and so on, has the factor 2 and is therefore not a prime number.
83545.m: In the sieve, you cross out the multiples of every prime you find.

83546.q: How many prime numbers are left when you use the Sieve of Eratosthenes for the numbers 1 to 100?
83546.e: Between 1 and 100 there are exactly 25 prime numbers, from 2 to 97.
83546.m: There are 25 prime numbers among the first hundred numbers.

83547.q: In the sieve up to 100, up to which prime do you have to cross out the multiples?
83547.e: You only have to check primes p where p · p is at most 100. 7 · 7 is 49, but 11 · 11 is already 121.
83547.m: You only sieve with primes whose square is not greater than the limit.

83548.q: From which number does it make sense to start crossing out the multiples of 5 in the sieve?
83548.e: The smaller multiples 10, 15 and 20 are already crossed out as multiples of 2 or 3. The first new multiple is 5 · 5, so 25.
83548.m: In the sieve, you start with the square of the prime.

83549.q: Which number is crossed out right at the start of the Sieve of Eratosthenes because it is not a prime?
83549.e: 1 has only one single factor and therefore does not count as a prime number.
83549.m: The sieve begins by crossing out the number 1.

83550.q: Which of these numbers stays in the Sieve of Eratosthenes up to 100?
83550.e: 87 = 3 · 29, 91 = 7 · 13 and 93 = 3 · 31 are crossed out. 89 has no factor except 1 and itself.
83550.m: Whatever remains in the sieve is a prime number.

83551.q: Eratosthenes is also famous for another achievement. Which one?
a: He built the first calculating machine
83551.e: Eratosthenes measured the position of the sun at two places in Egypt, Syene and Alexandria. From the difference and the distance he worked out the Earth’s circumference amazingly well.
83551.m: Eratosthenes worked out the size of the Earth more than 2000 years ago.

a: The sum of its proper factors equals the number
It is divisible by all numbers
83552.e: If you add up all the factors of a perfect number except the number itself, you get exactly the number again.
83552.m: A perfect number is as big as the sum of its proper factors.

83553.q: What is the smallest perfect number?
83553.e: The proper factors of 6 are 1, 2 and 3. Their sum is 6.
83553.m: Six is the smallest perfect number.

83554.q: What is the second smallest perfect number?
83554.e: The proper factors of 28 are 1, 2, 4, 7 and 14. Together they make 28.
83554.m: After six, 28 is the next perfect number.

83555.q: Which of these numbers is a perfect number?
83555.e: The proper factors of 496 are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31, 62, 124 and 248. Their sum is exactly 496.

83556.q: The proper factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6. Is 12 a perfect number?
a: No, the factor sum 16 is greater than 12
Yes, the factor sum is exactly 12
No, the factor sum 10 is less than 12
83556.e: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 makes 16. That is more than 12, so 12 is not perfect.
83556.m: A number is perfect only if the factor sum is exactly the number.

83557.q: What is the sum of the proper factors of 8?
83557.e: The proper factors of 8 are 1, 2 and 4. Their sum is 7, which is less than 8. So 8 is not perfect.
83557.m: For powers of two, the factor sum is always one less than the number.

83558.q: Which open question about perfect numbers is still unsolved today?
a: Whether there are odd perfect numbers
Whether perfect numbers exist at all
83558.e: All known perfect numbers are even. Nobody has yet been able to prove or disprove whether an odd one exists.
83558.m: Nobody knows to this day whether odd perfect numbers exist.

83559.q: The perfect numbers 6, 28, 496 and 8128: which digit do they end in?
83559.e: 6 and 496 end in 6, 28 and 8128 in 8. This is true of all even perfect numbers.
83559.m: Even perfect numbers always end in 6 or 8.

83560.q: Which of these numbers is a triangular number?
83560.e: 15 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5. You can lay 15 dots in a triangle with 5 rows.
83560.m: A triangular number is the sum of the numbers from 1 to n.

83561.e: The 10th triangular number is 1 + 2 + ... + 10, so 10 · 11 : 2, which makes 55.
83561.m: You calculate the nth triangular number as n times (n + 1) divided by 2.

83562.q: What is the sum of all the numbers from 1 to 100?
83562.e: You make pairs: 1 + 100, 2 + 99 and so on. There are 50 pairs adding up to 101, so 50 · 101, which makes 5050.
83562.m: With the pairing trick, you can add long rows of numbers in a flash.
