83933.q: Where does sweat come out of the skin?
83933.e: The skin has lots and lots of tiny openings, the pores. Sweat comes out there.
83933.m: Sweat comes out of tiny pores.

a: Small brown dots on the skin
83934.e: Freckles are small, light brown spots. They do not hurt.

83935.q: Why can you see freckles better in summer?
a: Because they get darker in summer
83935.e: Because of the sun, the skin makes more brown pigment. That is why the dots are easier to see in summer.

83936.q: Where do you often see freckles?
a: On the soles of the feet
83936.e: Freckles appear where a lot of sun shines on the skin. The face gets a particularly large amount of sun.
83936.m: Freckles are often on the face.

83937.q: Which people have freckles especially often?
a: People with fair skin and red hair
83937.e: Freckles are seen mainly on very fair skin. Red-haired people have them especially often.

83938.e: Freckles are small spots of colour. They are not an illness and not catching.

83939.q: Where does the tendency to have freckles come from?
a: It is inherited from your parents
83939.e: Whether you get freckles is inherited. That is why several people in one family often have them.
83939.m: The tendency to have freckles is inherited.

83940.q: What helps stop freckles getting even darker?
83940.e: Sunlight makes freckles darker. Sun cream and a hat protect the skin.

83941.q: What do freckles feel like when you run your finger over them?
a: Flat like the rest of the skin
83941.e: Freckles are just colour in the skin. That is why you cannot feel them; they are completely flat.
83941.m: Freckles are flat and you cannot feel them.

83942.e: A mole is a spot with lots of pigment cells. It is usually harmless.
83942.m: A mole is usually a harmless spot.

83943.q: What is another name for a mole?
83943.e: Mole and beauty spot usually mean the same thing. It is just a small coloured spot on the skin.
83943.m: A mole is also called a beauty spot.

83944.q: What should you do if a mole changes a lot?
83944.e: If a mole grows, itches or bleeds, a doctor should look at it. That way she can check whether everything is all right.
83944.m: Show changed moles to a doctor.

83945.q: Which change in a mole should you take seriously?
83945.e: A mole that grows quickly should be checked. Small, round moles that stay the same are usually harmless.
83945.m: Have a quickly growing mole checked.

83946.q: What is the doctor called who knows all about the skin?
83946.e: The dermatologist looks after the skin. She can also examine moles closely.
83946.m: The dermatologist looks after the skin.

83947.q: Can you wash off a mole?
a: No, it is in the skin
83947.e: The colour of a mole is inside the skin. That is why you cannot wash it off.
83947.m: You cannot wash off a mole.

83948.e: Most moles are light to dark brown. They contain a lot of brown pigment.

83949.q: Can new moles appear during your life?
a: Yes, especially in children and teenagers
83949.e: Many moles only appear during childhood and the teenage years. The sun can also play a part.

83950.q: What is often inside an inflamed spot?
83950.e: An inflamed spot often has a whitish dot. That is pus.
83950.m: There is often pus in an inflamed spot.

83951.q: Why should you not squeeze spots?
a: It can cause inflammation and scars
83951.e: Squeezing pushes germs deeper into the skin. Then it can get worse and leave marks.
83951.m: It is better not to squeeze spots.

83952.q: What can block the tiny holes in the skin so that a spot forms?
83952.e: The skin makes its own oil. If too much of it blocks a tiny hole in the skin, a spot can form.
83952.m: Too much skin oil can cause spots.

83953.q: Where do you get spots especially often?
a: On the soles of the feet
83953.e: The skin on the face has many glands that make skin oil. That is why spots appear there especially often.
83953.m: Spots often appear on the face.

83954.q: Who gets lots of spots especially often?
83954.e: In teenagers, the skin makes especially large amounts of skin oil. That is why many people of this age have spots.

83955.q: What is the skin condition with very many spots called?
83955.e: With acne, you have lots of spots, often on the face and back. A doctor can help with it.
83955.m: Acne is a skin condition with lots of spots.

83956.q: What is good for the skin when you have spots?
83956.e: Gentle washing removes extra oil and dirt. Scratching and rubbing only irritate the skin.
83956.m: With spots, wash your skin gently.

83957.q: What usually happens to a spot after a few days?
83957.e: Most spots disappear by themselves after a few days. The body heals them itself.

83958.q: How do you often get a graze?
83958.e: When you fall, your skin rubs over the rough ground. The top layer of skin is scraped off.
83958.m: When you fall, you often graze your skin.

83959.q: What do you do first with a dirty graze?
83959.e: First the dirt has to come out of the wound. To do this, you rinse it with clean water.

83960.q: What do you stick on a small graze?
83960.e: A plaster protects the wound from dirt. It has a soft pad in the middle.

83961.q: What forms on a graze when it heals?
83961.e: Dried blood and wound fluid form a hard crust. This crust is called a scab.
83961.m: A scab forms on a healing wound.

83962.q: Why should you not pick off the scab on a wound?
83962.e: New skin grows under the scab. If you pick it off, you disturb the healing.
83962.m: The scab protects the wound while it heals.

83963.q: Which part of the body is mainly injured in a graze?
83963.e: In a graze, only the top layer of skin is rubbed off. That is why it usually only bleeds a little.
83963.m: A graze injures the top layer of skin.

83964.q: What protects your knees from grazes when inline skating?
83964.e: Knee pads are hard pads over the knees. If you fall, the pad slides over the ground instead of your skin.
83964.m: Knee pads protect your knees when you fall.

83965.q: What can make a graze inflamed?
83965.e: If dirt and germs get into the wound, it can become inflamed. Then it goes red, warm and hurts more.
83965.m: Dirt and germs can make a wound inflamed.

83966.q: Where do children especially often get grazes when they fall?
83966.e: When you fall, you often catch yourself with your knees and arms. That is why knees and elbows are often grazed.
83966.m: Knees and elbows are often grazed.

83967.q: Which pet can scratch with its claws?
83967.e: Cats have sharp claws. When they defend themselves or play, they can scratch.
83967.m: Cats can scratch with their claws.

83968.q: What can easily give you a scratch on the hand when picking berries?
83968.e: Brambles have lots of small prickles. They easily scratch the skin.
83968.m: Thorny brambles can scratch the skin.

83969.q: What should you do after a cat scratch?
83969.e: Even a small scratch can contain germs. That is why you clean the spot well with soap and water.

83970.q: How can you stop yourself scratching until you bleed?
83970.e: Short fingernails are less sharp. That way you injure your skin less when you scratch.

a: A small, long injury to the skin
A round mark under the skin
A thick, hard patch of skin
83971.e: In a scratch, something sharp scrapes the skin open. That is why it is usually narrow and long.
83971.m: A scratch is a narrow scrape wound.

83972.q: Why should you not scratch an itchy spot until it bleeds?
a: Germs can get into the skin
83972.e: Scratching opens the skin. Then germs can get in and make the spot inflamed.
83972.m: Scratching until it bleeds lets germs in.

83973.q: Does a small, shallow scratch usually heal with or without a scar?
83973.e: In a small scratch, only the top layer of skin is injured. It usually grows back without a trace.
83973.m: Small scratches usually heal without a trace.

83974.q: What do people usually scratch themselves with?
83974.e: Fingernails are hard and have an edge. You use them to scratch yourself when you itch.
83974.m: We scratch ourselves with our fingernails.

a: From a knock or a blow
83975.e: When you knock yourself, the tissue under the skin is squashed. Afterwards you see a dark mark.
83975.m: A knock can cause a bruise.

83976.q: What has happened under the skin with a bruise?
83976.e: The knock tears tiny blood vessels. A little blood runs into the tissue and shows dark through the skin.
83976.m: Under a bruise, a little blood has leaked out.

83977.q: What is another word for a bruise?
83977.e: Haematoma is another word for a bruise. It often hurts a little when you press on it.
83977.m: A bruise is also called a haematoma.

83978.q: Which colours can a bruise turn as it heals?
83978.e: The body slowly breaks down the blood. As it does, the bruise changes colour through green to yellow.
83978.m: A healing bruise turns green and yellow.

83979.q: What helps against a bruise straight after a knock?
a: Bathing the spot in hot water
83979.e: Cold makes the blood vessels narrower. Then less blood leaks out and the bruise stays smaller.
83979.m: Cooling helps straight after a knock.

83980.q: Roughly how long does it take for a bruise to disappear?
83980.e: The body needs time to break down the blood. A bruise has usually gone after one to two weeks.
83980.m: A bruise disappears after about two weeks.

83981.q: Where do children get bruises especially often?
83981.e: On the shin, the bone lies directly under the skin. If you bump into something, you quickly get a bruise there.
83981.m: Bruises quickly appear on the shins.

83982.q: What do you call a swelling on the head after a knock?
83982.e: After a knock, the spot on the head swells up. A round swelling like this is called a bump.
83982.m: After a knock on the head, you often get a bump.

a: A place where a wound has healed
A brown dot from the sun
83983.e: When a wound heals, the body makes new tissue. Afterwards you can see this place as a scar.
83983.m: A scar is a healed wound.

83984.q: When is a scar more likely to be left behind?
83984.e: With deep wounds, the skin cannot grow back exactly the same. Then a scar is left.

83985.q: What colour is a fresh scar often?
83985.e: A fresh scar has a good blood supply. That is why it looks reddish at first.

83986.q: What does a scar usually become like over time?
83986.e: Over the months, a scar gets less blood. It becomes paler and flatter.

83987.q: Does hair grow on a scar?
a: Yes, but only after a year
83987.e: Scar tissue has no hair roots. That is why hair usually does not grow there.
83987.m: Hair usually does not grow on scars.

83988.q: Why should you protect a fresh scar from the sun?
a: So it does not turn dark
83988.e: Fresh scar tissue is sensitive to the sun. Otherwise it can turn brownish.
83988.m: Protect fresh scars from the sun.

83989.q: What helps a deep cut heal nicely?
83989.e: Stitching holds the edges of the wound together. Then only a narrow scar is left.

83990.q: How long does a scar usually last?
83990.e: Scar tissue never completely disappears. It can become paler, but usually stays visible.

83991.q: What is the pigment called that colours the skin brown?
83991.e: Special cells in the skin make melanin. The more of it there is, the darker the skin.

83992.q: What colour does fair skin go with sunburn?
83992.e: With sunburn, the skin is inflamed. It goes red, hot and sore.

83993.q: Why do people have different skin colours?
a: Their skin makes different amounts of pigment
They wash a different number of times
They sleep for different lengths of time
83993.e: How much pigment the skin makes is inherited. This results in many different skin tones.
83993.m: Skin colour depends on the pigment in the skin.

83994.q: What does dark skin protect against better than fair skin?
83994.e: Lots of pigment in the skin blocks some of the sun’s rays. That is why dark skin gets sunburnt less often.
83994.m: Dark skin is better protected from the sun.

83995.q: What do you call the brown colour of the skin after days in the sun?
83995.e: In the sun, the skin makes more pigment to protect itself. This makes it go brown.
83995.m: In the sun, the skin gets a suntan.

83996.q: At what time of day is the summer sun strongest for the skin?
83996.e: Around midday, the sun is at its highest. Then its rays are strongest, so you look for shade.
83996.m: In summer, look for shade around midday.

83997.q: What is it called when your face goes red with embarrassment?
83997.e: When you are embarrassed, more blood flows into your cheeks. That is why your face goes red.
83997.m: People who are embarrassed often blush.

83998.q: What does the skin often look like when you are ill or get a big fright?
83998.e: With a fright or illness, less blood flows through the skin. Then it looks pale.
83998.m: With a fright, the skin often goes pale.

a: Lines and furrows in the skin
83999.e: Wrinkles are lines where the skin folds. You see them on the forehead, for example.
83999.m: Wrinkles are lines in the skin.

84000.q: Why does the skin get wrinkles in old age?
84000.e: Young skin is firm and springs back. In old age it becomes less elastic, so wrinkles stay.

84001.q: What happens to your fingers when you stay in the bath for a long time?
84001.e: After a long bath, the fingertips get lots of little wrinkles. This soon goes away after drying off.
84001.m: After a long bath, your fingers go wrinkly.

84002.q: What is another name for fine wrinkles at the outer corner of the eye?
84002.e: The fine lines at the corner of the eye spread out like a bird’s toes. That is why they are called crow’s feet.
84002.m: Fine lines at the corner of the eye are called crow’s feet.

84003.q: What makes the skin get wrinkly faster?
84003.e: Strong sun damages the skin over time. Then it gets wrinkles earlier.
84003.m: Too much sun makes the skin wrinkly faster.

84004.q: What are the vertical lines between the eyebrows called?
84004.e: When you look cross, you pull your eyebrows together. This creates vertical lines between them.
84004.m: Frown lines are between the eyebrows.

84005.q: Who usually has the most wrinkles on their face?
84005.e: The older a person is, the more wrinkles they usually have. Children have hardly any wrinkles.

84006.q: Which animal is known for its thick, wrinkly skin?
84006.e: An elephant’s skin has lots of deep furrows. Water and mud stay in them, which cools it down.

84007.q: What often forms on a toe when a shoe presses on it for a long time?
84007.e: A corn is a small, hard thickening of hard skin. It forms from pressure, for example from shoes that are too tight.
84007.m: Tight shoes can cause a corn.

84008.q: Why does the skin form hard skin?
a: To protect itself from lots of pressure and rubbing
84008.e: Where the skin is often pressed and rubbed, it makes itself thicker. That way it protects itself.
84008.m: Hard skin protects the skin from lots of pressure.

84009.q: What helps keep hard skin on the feet soft?
a: Wearing shoes that are too tight
84009.e: Foot cream gives the skin moisture and oil. Then the hard skin stays softer.

84010.q: Is hard skin on the feet dangerous?
a: No, it is usually natural protection
Yes, it bleeds all the time
84010.e: Hard skin is thick, firm skin. Normally it protects the foot and is completely natural.
84010.m: Hard skin is usually natural protection.

84011.q: What does hard skin feel like?
84011.e: Hard skin is made of many layers of firm skin cells. That is why it feels hard and rough.
84011.m: Hard skin is hard and rough.

84012.q: What can you use to gently rub off thick hard skin on your feet?
84012.e: A pumice stone is a light, rough stone. You can use it to carefully rub off hard skin.
84012.m: You rub off hard skin with a pumice stone.

84013.q: What do you call a patch of hard skin on the hands, for example from rowing?
84013.e: When hands often grip tightly, hard skin forms there. These hard patches are called calluses.
84013.m: Hard patches on the hands are called calluses.

84014.q: Why can you feel less through thick hard skin?
a: It is made of dead skin cells
84014.e: Hard skin is made of cells that are no longer alive. That is why you feel less there.
84014.m: Hard skin is made of dead cells.

84015.q: What can develop with very thick, dry hard skin on the heel?
84015.e: Very thick, dry hard skin is no longer bendy. It can split open, and that hurts.
84015.m: Hard skin that is too thick can crack.

84016.q: Why does a mosquito bite itch?
84016.e: When it bites, the mosquito puts a little saliva into the skin. The body reacts to it, and it itches.
84016.m: The mosquito’s saliva causes the itching.

84017.e: Only the females bite. They need blood so that their eggs can grow.

84018.q: When do mosquitoes especially like to bite in our part of the world?
a: In the evening and at night
84018.e: Many mosquitoes are out and about at dusk and at night. That is why they often buzz around as you fall asleep.
84018.m: Mosquitoes often bite in the evening and at night.

84019.q: Where do mosquitoes lay their eggs?
84019.e: Mosquito larvae live in water. That is why the females lay their eggs on or near water, for example in ponds, puddles or water butts.
84019.m: Mosquitoes lay their eggs on or next to water.

84020.q: What helps against the itching of a mosquito bite?
84020.e: Cold calms the skin, and the itching gets less. Scratching, on the other hand, only makes it worse.

84021.q: What protects you from mosquito bites at night?
84021.e: A mosquito net hangs over the bed like a fine tent. The mosquitoes cannot get through.
84021.m: A mosquito net keeps mosquitoes away.

84022.q: What does a mosquito bite usually look like?
84022.e: After the bite, the skin swells up a little at that spot. It goes red and itches.
84022.m: A mosquito bite is a small red swelling.

84023.q: What attracts mosquitoes to us humans?
84023.e: Mosquitoes smell the air we breathe out and our body smell. That way they find us even in the dark.
84023.m: Mosquitoes find us by our breath and smell.

84024.q: What does a mosquito bite with?
a: With a sting on its rear end
84024.e: The mosquito has a thin tube-like mouthpart on its head. It uses it to pierce the skin and suck.
84024.m: The mosquito bites with its mouthpart.

84025.q: What is the force called that slows things down when two surfaces rub against each other?
84025.e: When two things slide along each other, friction holds back the movement. Rough surfaces rub more strongly than smooth ones.
84025.m: Friction slows things down when surfaces rub against each other.

84026.e: Rough surfaces have lots of tiny bumps. These catch on each other and slow things down more.
84026.m: Rough surfaces have more friction than smooth ones.

84028.q: Why does a toy car roll less far on a carpet than on a wooden floor?
a: The carpet slows it down more
84028.e: The soft fibres of the carpet slow the wheels down. On a smooth wooden floor the car rolls more easily.
84028.m: A carpet slows things down more than a smooth floor.

84029.q: Which trousers let you go down a slide fastest?
84029.e: Smooth fabric glides better over the slide. Rough or rubberised fabrics slow you down.

84030.q: What happens to a bike on a flat road when you stop pedalling?
a: It keeps going at the same speed for ever
84030.e: Friction at the wheels and air resistance slow the bike down. Without pedalling, it gets slower.
84030.m: Without power, friction slows the bike down.

84031.q: Why do we need friction when walking?
a: So that our feet do not slip
So that we get tired faster
So that our shoes stay clean
84031.e: When walking, we push off from the ground. Without friction our feet would slip away as on ice.
84031.m: Without friction we could not walk.

84032.q: Between which things is there friction when you write with a pencil?
a: Between the lead and the paper
Between the lead and the air
Between the paper and the light
Between the table and the ceiling
84032.e: The lead rubs over the paper. Fine particles stick to the paper, and that makes the writing.
84032.m: When writing, the lead rubs on the paper.

84033.q: Why is it easier to pull a sledge over snow than over a meadow?
a: On snow the friction is smaller
On snow the sledge is heavier
84033.e: Smooth snow slows the runners only a little. Grass and soil are rougher and slow them down more.
84033.m: A sledge glides easily on snow.

84034.q: Why does a table tennis bat have a rubber covering?
a: So that it grips the ball well
So that the bat is lighter
So that the ball bounces more quietly
84034.e: Rubber has a lot of friction. The ball sticks to the covering for a moment, so you can steer and spin it well.
84034.m: The rubber covering grips the ball.

a: When rain falls on frozen ground
When the sun shines in summer
When it is foggy in autumn
84035.e: If rain falls on very cold ground, it freezes at once. A thin, smooth layer of ice forms.
84035.m: Rain on frozen ground turns into black ice.

84036.q: Why is black ice especially treacherous?
a: You often can hardly see it
84036.e: Black ice is thin and transparent. The road just looks wet, but it is as slippery as glass.
84036.m: You often cannot see black ice.

84037.q: Which animal is a good example to follow when walking on ice?
84037.e: Penguins waddle with small steps and keep their weight over their feet. This way you slip less on ice.
84037.m: On ice, walk like a penguin.

84038.q: Why is ice especially slippery when it is wet?
a: There is a thin film of water on it
It is then warmer than 20 degrees
84038.e: A film of water on the ice acts like a lubricant. It makes the friction even smaller.

84040.q: What should drivers do when there is black ice?
a: Drive closer to the car in front
84040.e: On black ice the tyres have little grip. The braking distance becomes much longer, so you drive slowly.
84040.m: On black ice you drive slowly.

84041.q: What is often spread on roads so that the ice melts?
84041.e: Salt makes ice melt even a little below 0 degrees. That is why salt is spread on the roads in winter.

84042.q: Which shoes help most on black ice?
84042.e: Spikes are small metal points under the sole. They dig into the ice and give grip.

84043.q: What are the blades of an ice skate usually made of?
84043.e: Blades are made of hard steel. It stays sharp for a long time and glides well over the ice.
84043.m: Ice skate blades are made of steel.

84044.q: Why do ice skates glide so well over the ice?
a: There is very little friction between blade and ice
84044.e: Ice is very smooth. The smooth blade glides over it with very little friction.
84044.m: On ice, blades glide with little friction.

84045.q: Where can you skate safely in winter in many Swiss towns and villages?
84045.e: At an ice rink the ice is smooth and safe. Many municipalities have an artificial ice rink or an ice field in winter.
84045.m: At the ice rink you can skate safely.

84046.q: What is important about a skate blade so that you do not slide sideways on a bend?
84046.e: The sharp edges cut a little into the ice. That way the blade holds on the bend.
84046.m: Sharp blade edges give grip on bends.

84047.q: Which team sport is played on ice skates?
84047.e: In ice hockey, the players skate and play with a puck. Ice hockey is very popular in Switzerland.
84047.m: Ice hockey is played on ice skates.

84048.q: What is the sport called in which you show jumps and pirouettes on ice skates?
84048.e: In figure skating, you show jumps, spins and steps to music. It is a sport at the Winter Olympics.
84048.m: In figure skating you show jumps on the ice.

84049.q: What must you pay attention to when skating on a frozen lake?
a: Only go onto thick ice that has been declared safe
Go onto thin ice if possible
Always go onto the ice alone
Only go onto the ice at night
84049.e: Thin ice can break, and that is extremely dangerous. That is why you only go onto the ice when it has been declared safe.
84049.m: Only step onto ice that has been declared safe.

84050.q: Why can't you glide on tarmac with ice skates?
a: The friction there is far too great
84050.e: Tarmac is rough and slows the blade down strongly. That is why ice skates only glide on smooth ice.
84050.m: Blades do not glide on rough tarmac.

84051.q: Why do you sink less deeply into the snow on skis than in shoes?
a: The weight is spread over a large area
84051.e: Skis are long and wide. So your body weight presses on a larger area, and you sink in less.
84051.m: Large areas sink less into the snow.

84052.q: What do some cross-country skis have under the middle so that they do not slip back when you push off?
84052.e: The scales are like tiny steps in the base. Forwards they glide, backwards they grip.
84052.m: Skis with scales do not slip back.

84053.q: On a ski tour, what do you stick under your skis so that you do not slip back going uphill?
84053.e: Climbing skins have little hairs that point backwards. They let the skis glide forwards but brake them backwards.
84053.m: With skins you can go uphill.

84054.q: What is the braking position for beginners called, with the ski tips together?
84054.e: In the snowplough, the skis form a V. The edges press into the snow and brake.

84055.q: In which mountain range are most of Switzerland's ski resorts?
84055.e: Most Swiss ski resorts are in the Alps. There are high mountains with lots of snow there.
84055.m: Most Swiss ski resorts are in the Alps.

84056.q: Why do skis have sharp steel edges at the sides?
a: So that they grip on turns
84056.e: On a turn, you tilt the ski onto its edge. The sharp edge cuts into the snow and holds.
84056.m: Ski edges give grip on turns.

84057.q: What does a ski racer do to go faster in the downhill?
84057.e: In a crouch, the body offers less surface to the air. So the skier is slowed down less.
84057.m: In a crouch you go faster.

84058.q: Why is sand spread on icy paths in winter?
a: So that you have more grip
So that the ice gets warmer
So that the birds have food
84058.e: The hard grains of sand make the smooth ice rough. So feet and tyres slip less.
84058.m: Sand on ice gives more grip.

a: No, it only makes it rougher
84059.e: Sand does not thaw the ice. It simply lies on top and increases the friction.
84059.m: Sand does not melt ice; it makes it rough.

84060.q: What is used to spread road salt on big roads?
84060.e: A gritter has a spreading disc at the back. It spins and spreads the salt evenly on the road.
84060.m: A gritter spreads salt on the road.

84061.q: Why do some places prefer to spread sand or grit rather than salt?
a: Salt can harm plants and soil
84061.e: Salty water gets into the soil at the side of the road. This can harm trees and other plants.

84062.q: What is done with the grit on the roads in spring?
a: It is left there for ever
84062.e: When winter is over, the grit is no longer needed. Road sweepers sweep it off the roads.
84062.m: In spring the grit is swept away.

84063.q: What do many locomotives have so that their wheels do not spin on slippery rails?
84063.e: On wet or slippery rails, the locomotive spreads sand in front of the wheels. So the wheels grip better.
84063.m: Locomotives spread sand for more grip.

84064.q: Who spreads sand and salt on a municipality's roads in winter?
84064.e: The winter road service clears snow and grits paths and roads. It often sets off very early in the morning.
84064.m: The winter road service grits the roads.

84065.q: Why is sand better than flour for spreading on ice?
a: Grains of sand are hard and rough
84065.e: Hard, sharp grains of sand press into the ice and stay rough. Flour would get wet and slimy.
84065.m: Hard grains of sand give grip on ice.

84066.q: Why do walking boots have a chunky tread on the sole?
84066.e: The deep grooves grip soil, stones and snow. So you slip less on the footpath.
84066.m: A chunky tread gives good grip.

84067.q: What material are many shoe soles made of?
84067.e: Rubber is bendy and has a lot of friction on the ground. That is why many soles are made of rubber.
84067.m: Many shoe soles are made of rubber.

84068.q: With which sole are you more likely to slip?
84068.e: Without tread, the sole has less grip. Especially on a wet floor you slip easily.

84069.q: Which shoes do football players wear on grass?
84069.e: Studs dig into the grass. So the players can start quickly and change direction.
84069.m: Football boots have studs for the grass.

84070.q: What happens to the tread of a sole when you wear the shoe for a long time?
84070.e: With every step, the sole rubs on the ground. Slowly it wears away.
84070.m: The tread of a sole wears away over time.

84071.q: Why do you slip easily in socks on a wooden floor?
a: Socks are smooth and have little grip
84071.e: Fabric on smooth wood has only a little friction. That is why you slip quickly in socks.
84071.m: Socks slip on a smooth floor.

84072.q: What do non-slip socks have on the bottom?
84072.e: Small rubber dots increase the friction on the floor. So you do not slip in these socks.

84073.q: Which shoes are best on a climbing wall?
a: Climbing shoes with soft rubber soles
84073.e: The soft rubber sole sticks even to small footholds. So you get good grip on the wall.
84073.m: Climbing shoes grip thanks to soft rubber.

84074.e: The tread is the grooves and patterns on the surface of the tyre. They make sure it grips the road well.
84074.m: Tyre tread is the grooves in the tyre.

84075.q: What do the grooves in a tyre do when it rains?
84075.e: The grooves lead the water to the side. So the tyre stays in contact with the road.

84076.q: What is it called when a car slides on a film of water and can no longer be steered?
84076.e: In aquaplaning, the tyre floats on the water. It no longer touches the road, and steering and braking hardly work.
84076.m: In aquaplaning the tyre floats on the water.

84077.q: Which tyres are best on snow?
84077.e: Winter tyres have lots of fine cuts and a softer rubber mix. So they grip better on snow and ice.
84077.m: In winter you drive with winter tyres.

84078.q: What do you put around car tyres on mountain roads when there is a lot of snow?
84078.e: Metal snow chains grip snow and ice. On some mountain pass roads they are even compulsory when there is snow.
84078.m: Snow chains give grip on snow.

84079.q: Why do mountain bikes have chunky, knobbly tyres?
84079.e: The chunky knobs grip soil, roots and stones. So the mountain bike slips less in the forest.

84080.q: Why do racing bikes have narrow, almost smooth tyres?
a: So that they roll easily on the road
So that they grip well in mud
So that they hold in snow
So that they jump over stones
84080.e: Smooth, narrow tyres have little rolling resistance on tarmac. That is why a racing bike goes easily and fast.

84081.q: What must you do with a tyre whose tread is completely worn down?
84081.e: Without tread, a tyre has hardly any grip in the wet. That is why it must be replaced.

84082.q: Which tyres have especially chunky and deep lugs?
84082.e: Tractors often drive on soft fields. Big, deep lugs grip the soil and pull the tractor forwards.

84083.q: Why does a wet bar of soap slip out of your hand easily?
a: Soap and water make it slippery
84083.e: Wet soap forms a slippery film. This makes the friction between your hand and the soap very small.

84084.q: What should you do if soapy water has run onto the floor?
84084.e: Soapy water makes the floor very slippery. That is why you wipe it up at once so that nobody falls.
84084.m: Wipe up soapy water on the floor at once.

84085.q: How can soap help you pull a tight ring off your finger?
84085.e: Soap reduces the friction between the ring and the skin. Then the ring is easier to pull off.
84085.m: Soap helps pull off a tight ring.

84086.q: What forms when you rub soap hard with water?
84086.e: Soapy water traps lots of little air bubbles. This makes foam.

84087.q: Why do people often put a non-slip mat in the shower?
a: Soapy water makes the floor slippery
The mat makes the water warm
84087.e: You slip easily on the wet, soapy floor. The mat has little bumps and gives your feet grip.
84087.m: A non-slip mat gives grip in the shower.

84088.q: What does soap help with when you wash your hands?
84088.e: Soap loosens grease and dirt from the skin. The water then rinses them away, together with many germs.

84089.q: How long should you wash your hands with soap?
84089.e: You should soap your hands thoroughly for about 20 to 30 seconds. This removes most germs.
84089.m: Wash your hands for about half a minute.

84090.q: What is soap traditionally made from?
84090.e: Soap is made by boiling fat or oil with lye. People have made soap this way for a very long time.
84090.m: Soap is made from fat or oil.

84091.q: What gets hot when you drill a hole in a wall?
84091.e: The drill bit rubs its way through the hard wall as it turns. Its tip gets very hot.
84091.m: When drilling, the drill bit gets hot.

84092.q: When do many people rub their hands together?
84092.e: When it is cold, you want to warm your hands. Rubbing makes a little heat.
84092.m: When it is cold, you rub your hands.

84093.q: What can happen if you slide quickly over a carpet on bare knees?
a: The skin gets hot and sore
The skin goes blue and cold
84093.e: When you slide quickly, your skin rubs hard on the carpet. It gets hot and can be rubbed sore.
84093.m: Hard rubbing can make your skin sore.

84094.q: How did people make fire in the past without matches?
84094.e: If you rub wood together very fast, it gets hot. Then dry material can start to glow.
84094.m: Rubbing wood together quickly can make fire.

84095.q: What gets warm when you saw wood?
84095.e: The saw blade rubs on the wood with every stroke. This makes it warm.
84095.m: When sawing, the saw blade gets warm.

84096.q: Why do your hands get hot when you slide down a rope quickly?
a: Because of the friction on the rope
Because the rope was lying in the sun
84096.e: Your hands rub hard on the rope as you slide. This makes the skin hot, so it is better to climb down hand over hand.
84096.m: Sliding quickly down a rope makes your hands hot.

84097.q: What gets warm when you rub out something for a long time and hard?
84097.e: The rubber rubs hard over the paper. It gets noticeably warm.
84097.m: When rubbing out, the rubber gets warm.

84098.q: What is the heat called that is produced by rubbing?
84098.e: When two things rub against each other, movement turns into heat. This heat is called frictional heat.

84100.q: Why does the head of a match catch fire when you strike it?
84100.e: When you strike it along the striking surface, the head rubs hard. The substances in the head get hot and catch fire.
84100.m: Friction lights the head of a match.

84101.q: Where does a safety match light?
a: Only on the striking surface of the box
84101.e: Part of the chemicals for lighting are on the striking surface of the box. Only there can the safety match light.
84101.m: Safety matches only light on the box.

84102.q: What should you do with a used match?
a: Throw it away while it is burning
Put it in the bin while it is glowing
84102.e: A glowing match can still start a fire. That is why you put it out completely before throwing it away.
84102.m: Always put a match out completely.

84103.q: Why is a wet match hard to light?
a: The head does not get hot enough
84103.e: The water in the head absorbs the heat. So the head does not get hot enough to burn.
84103.m: Wet matches are hard to light.

84104.q: Who should be there when children light a match?
84104.e: Fire can become dangerous. That is why children only light matches when an adult is there.
84104.m: Children only light fires with adults.

84105.q: What is Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale about a poor girl who sells matches called?
84105.e: Hans Christian Andersen was a Danish writer of fairy tales. In this tale, a poor girl sells matches on a cold winter night.
84105.m: Andersen wrote the fairy tale of the little match girl.

84106.q: On a bike with rim brakes, what presses against the wheel?
84106.e: When you pull the brake lever, two brake pads press against the rim. This slows the wheel.
84106.m: Brake pads press against the rim.

84107.q: What are the brake pads on a bike usually made of?
84107.e: Rubber has a lot of friction on the rim. That is why rubber pads brake well.
84107.m: Bike brake pads are usually made of rubber.

84108.q: How does a brake pad slow down the bike?
a: It blows air at the wheel
It makes the wheel turn faster
84108.e: The brake pad rubs against the turning rim. The friction slows the wheel down.

84109.q: Why do rim brakes work less well in the rain?
a: The wet rim is more slippery
The rain makes the bike heavier
The rain blows against the bike
84109.e: Water on the rim makes the friction smaller. That is why the braking distance is longer in the wet.
84109.m: In the rain a bike brakes less well.

84110.q: What happens to brake pads over time?
a: They go soft like cotton wool
84110.e: Every time you brake, a little rubber wears away. That is why worn brake pads must be replaced.

84111.q: What should you quickly check on a bike before a ride?
84111.e: Good brakes are very important on a bike. You briefly pull both brake levers and check whether the pads hold the wheel firmly.
84111.m: Check the brakes before a ride.

84112.q: What do you put behind the wheels of a lorry parked on a slope?
84112.e: A wedge is pushed in front of or behind the wheel. It stops the vehicle from rolling away.
84112.m: A wedge holds a vehicle in place on a slope.

84113.q: Which noise do worn bike brakes often make?
84113.e: When brake pads are worn or dirty, they often squeal when braking. Then you should have them checked.

84114.q: What do you put on a dry bike chain?
84114.e: Oil makes the chain run smoothly. It then runs more quietly and easily.
84114.m: You look after a bike chain with oil.

84115.q: What can you rub on a stuck zip so that it runs better?
84115.e: A pencil lead contains graphite. Graphite is a dry lubricant and makes the zip slide more easily.
84115.m: Graphite from a pencil is a lubricant.

84116.q: What helps with a squeaky door?
a: A few drops of oil on the hinges
84116.e: The squeak comes from friction in the hinge. A little oil makes the hinge quiet again.
84116.m: Oil on the hinge stops the squeak.

84117.q: What does a car engine need so that its parts run well?
84117.e: In the engine, many metal parts move very fast. Engine oil reduces the friction and protects them.

84118.q: Which lubricant is thick and sticky like a paste?
84118.e: Grease is thick and stays in place well. It is used, for example, for bearings and joints on machines.
84118.m: Grease is thick like a paste.

84119.q: What happens to a bike chain that is never looked after?
a: It runs stiffly and wears out
It gets longer and more colourful
84119.e: Without care, metal rubs on metal. The chain runs stiffly, rusts more easily and wears out faster.
84119.m: A chain that is looked after lasts longer.

84120.q: What acts like a lubricant in our joints?
84120.e: There is a thick fluid in every joint. It lets the bones slide smoothly against each other.

84121.q: What can you use to make a sticking wooden drawer slide more easily?
84121.e: You rub candle wax on the runners of the drawer. The wax reduces the friction, and it slides more easily.
84121.m: Candle wax makes drawers run smoothly.

84122.q: In which direction does a large rocket take off?
84122.e: Large rockets take off straight up and only tilt to the side later. That way they leave the thick air most quickly.
84122.m: A large rocket takes off straight up.

84123.q: What is the moment called when a rocket leaves the ground?
84123.e: At lift-off the rocket leaves the launch pad.
84123.m: When the rocket leaves the ground, it lifts off.

84124.q: Where do astronauts sit during a rocket launch?
a: In a capsule on top of the rocket
Right at the bottom by the engine
In the middle of the fuel tank
Next to the rocket on the pad
84124.e: The capsule with the astronauts sits on top of the rocket. Below it are the tanks and the engines.
84124.m: The astronauts fly in a capsule on top of the rocket.

84125.q: Why is a rocket launch often postponed during a thunderstorm?
a: Because lightning could strike the rocket
Because rain puts out the fuel
Because thunder knocks the rocket over
Because you cannot film in the rain
84125.e: A lightning strike can damage the rocket's electronics. That is why people wait for better weather.
84125.m: In a thunderstorm, a rocket had better stay on the ground.

84126.q: What is the place called where experts monitor a rocket flight on screens?
84126.e: In the control centre, lots of experts sit at screens. They monitor the flight and talk to the astronauts.
84126.m: Every rocket flight is closely monitored in the control centre.

84127.q: How fast must a rocket fly so that it can orbit the Earth?
84127.e: A rocket has to get incredibly fast, much faster than any aeroplane. Otherwise it falls back to Earth.
84127.m: A rocket must be very fast so that it does not fall back to Earth.

84128.q: What can you hear near a rocket that is taking off?
84128.e: The engines burn huge amounts of fuel in a short time. That makes a deafening noise.
84128.m: A rocket launch is incredibly loud.

84129.q: Why are spectators not allowed close to the rocket at launch?
a: Because it is too loud and too dangerous
Because otherwise the rocket will not start
Because you cannot see anything from close up
84129.e: Heat, noise and the risk of an explosion are very great near the pad. So spectators usually stand several kilometres away.
84129.m: Spectators watch a rocket launch from a safe distance.

84130.q: What is the path called on which a satellite circles the Earth after launch?
84130.e: In its orbit, a satellite flies round and round the Earth.
84130.m: A satellite circles the Earth in its orbit.

84131.q: What is the place called from which a rocket takes off?
84131.e: The rocket stands ready on the launch pad. It lifts off from there.
84131.m: A rocket takes off from the launch pad.

84132.q: How does a rocket stand on the launch pad?
84132.e: The rocket stands upright with its tip pointing up. That way it can climb straight into the sky.
84132.m: On the launch pad the rocket stands upright.

84133.q: What is the tall tower next to a rocket on the launch pad for?
a: People use it to reach the rocket
It is a viewing tower for guests
It holds the rocket during flight
It is a lighthouse for ships
84133.e: Astronauts and technicians climb into the rocket from the tower. Pipes and cables for electricity and fuel also run through it.
84133.m: Astronauts reach their capsule via the launch tower.

84134.q: Where are the flames under the rocket directed at launch?
a: Into a trench under the pad
84134.e: Under many launch pads there is a flame trench. It steers the hot gases away from the rocket.
84134.m: A flame trench leads the fire away from the rocket.

84135.q: Why does a lot of water pour over the launch pad at launch?
a: To dampen noise and protect the pad
To wash the rocket before the flight
To water the grass around it
84135.e: The water absorbs part of the noise and cools the pad. Otherwise the sound waves could damage the rocket.
84135.m: Water dampens the tremendous noise at launch.

84136.q: How does a large rocket get from the assembly building to the launch pad?
84136.e: Large rockets are driven slowly to the pad on huge crawler vehicles or rail wagons. The Soyuz, for example, travels lying down on the railway.
84136.m: A rocket is moved slowly and carefully to the launch pad.

84137.q: What happens to a launch pad after a launch?
84137.e: Heat and pressure damage the pad a little at every launch. Afterwards it is checked and got ready for the next launch.
84137.m: A launch pad is repaired after every launch.

84138.q: Why are launch pads built from very thick concrete and steel?
a: Because the fire from the engines is extremely hot
84138.e: The exhaust gases of the engines are thousands of degrees hot and very powerful. Only thick concrete and steel can withstand that.
84138.m: A launch pad must withstand fire and tremendous forces.

84139.q: What is the part called at the back of the rocket that the fire streams out of?
84139.e: The nozzle is like a large funnel. It directs the hot gases backwards.
84139.m: The rocket's hot gases stream out of the nozzle.

84140.q: What is the force called with which an engine pushes the rocket forwards?
84140.e: Thrust is the force produced by the engine. The greater the thrust, the more strongly the rocket accelerates.
84140.m: The engine gives the rocket thrust.

84141.q: Where does the fuel burn in a rocket engine?
84141.e: In the combustion chamber the propellants mix and burn. The hot gases then stream out through the nozzle.
84141.m: The fuel burns in the combustion chamber.

84142.q: About how hot do the gases in a rocket engine get?
84142.e: Temperatures of around 3000 degrees are produced in the combustion chamber. That is hotter than liquid lava.
84142.m: A rocket engine gets hotter than a volcano.

84143.q: Where is a rocket's main engine usually located?
a: Right at the top in the tip
On the side in the middle
At the front on the nose
84143.e: The main engine sits at the bottom at the tail. That way it pushes the gases downwards and pushes the rocket upwards.
84143.m: A rocket's engine sits at the bottom.

84144.q: How can a rocket change direction during flight?
a: It swivels the nozzle a little
84144.e: Many engines can be tilted a little. Then the thrust pushes slightly at an angle and the rocket changes direction.
84144.m: A rocket steers by swivelling its nozzle.

84145.q: What are small thrusters on a spacecraft for?
a: To turn and steer it in space
84145.e: Small thrusters give short bursts. They can be used to turn a spacecraft or to move it precisely up to a space station.
84145.m: Small thrusters let you steer a spacecraft precisely.

84146.q: What happens when an engine runs out of fuel?
84146.e: Without fuel nothing can burn any more. The engine goes out and gives no more thrust.
84146.m: Without fuel an engine shuts off.

84147.q: Why are large rockets made of several stages?
a: So empty parts fall away and it gets lighter
So it takes off more quietly
84147.e: When a stage is empty, it is dropped. The rocket then has less weight to carry and gets faster.
84147.m: A rocket drops empty stages to become lighter.

84148.q: What does the next stage do when the empty lower stage has fallen away?
a: It flies back to the launch pad
84148.e: After separation, the next stage fires its engine. That way the rocket keeps flying without a break.
84148.m: Once the lower stage is gone, the next stage fires.

84149.q: What do you call a rocket made of several parts stacked on top of each other?
84149.e: In a multistage rocket, several rocket parts are built on top of each other. Each stage has its own tanks and engines.
84149.m: A multistage rocket has several parts on top of each other.

84150.q: Where do dropped rocket stages often fall?
84150.e: Many rockets fly over the sea. There, empty stages can fall into the water without danger to people.
84150.m: Empty rocket stages often fall into the sea.

84151.q: What are the extra rockets attached to the sides of the main rocket called?
84151.e: Boosters give extra thrust at launch. Once they have burnt out, they are dropped.
84151.m: Boosters give the rocket extra power at launch.

84152.q: Which stage of a rocket fires first at launch?
84152.e: The bottom stage is the biggest and most powerful. It lifts the whole rocket off the ground.
84152.m: At launch the bottom stage works first.

84153.q: Why are some rocket parts landed vertically again today?
a: So they can be used again
So they fly on to the Moon
So they can be put in a museum
So they are easier to scrap
84153.e: A rocket stage is very expensive. If it lands in one piece, it can be used again for another flight.
84153.m: A landed rocket stage can fly again.

84154.q: Which part of a multistage rocket flies the furthest?
84154.e: The top stage carries the payload all the way to its destination. The lower stages fall back earlier.
84154.m: The top stage flies the furthest.

84155.q: What happens if you let go of a blown-up balloon without tying it?
a: It stays still in the air
84155.e: The air streams backwards out of the balloon. This pushes the balloon forwards.
84155.m: An open balloon flies off by recoil.

84156.q: What principle does a rocket fly by?
84156.e: The rocket pushes gases out backwards. In reaction it moves forwards.
84156.m: A rocket flies thanks to recoil.

84157.q: You are standing on a skateboard and throw a heavy ball forwards. What happens to you?
84157.e: When you push the ball forwards, it pushes you backwards. That is recoil.
84157.m: If you throw something forwards, you are pushed backwards.

84158.q: Which scientist described that every force has an equal opposite force?
84158.e: Isaac Newton described this law over 300 years ago. It is also known as “action equals reaction”.
84158.m: Every force has an opposite force, said Isaac Newton.

84159.q: Which sea creature swims by recoil, pushing out water?
84159.e: A squid sucks in water and squeezes it out hard. That way it shoots off like a little rocket.
84159.m: The squid swims by recoil like a rocket.

84160.q: What do firefighters feel when lots of water shoots out of their hose?
84160.e: The water shoots forwards, so the hose pushes backwards. The firefighters have to hold it tightly.
84160.m: A fire hose pushes backwards because of recoil.

84161.q: You are sitting in a rowing boat and throw a heavy sack onto the bank. Which way does the boat move?
84161.e: The sack flies towards the bank, so the boat is pushed the opposite way. That is recoil.
84161.m: When you throw something, a boat moves the opposite way.

84162.q: Why does a lawn sprinkler with bent arms spin round?
a: Because of the recoil of the water
84162.e: The water sprays out of the arms at an angle. The recoil pushes the arms the other way, so they spin.
84162.m: A lawn sprinkler spins because of the recoil of the water.

84163.q: Does a rocket need air to push against?
a: No, it pushes against its exhaust gases
Yes, without air it cannot fly
No, it is pulled by the Moon
84163.e: The rocket pushes its exhaust gases backwards and they push the rocket forwards. That is why it can fly even in airless space.
84163.m: A rocket does not need air to push against.

84164.q: What is a water rocket often made from?
84164.e: A plastic bottle is light and withstands air pressure well. That is why it is good for a water rocket.
84164.m: A water rocket is made from a plastic bottle.

84165.q: What do you use to pump air into a water rocket?
84165.e: With the bicycle pump you push more and more air into the bottle. The pressure in the bottle rises.
84165.m: You pump up a water rocket with a bicycle pump.

84166.q: What sprays downwards when a water rocket takes off?
84166.e: The squashed air forces the water out downwards hard. This makes the bottle shoot upwards.
84166.m: Water sprays downwards from a water rocket.

84167.q: Why do you only partly fill a water rocket with water?
a: So there is room for compressed air
So it is easier to carry
So the water does not freeze
84167.e: The air in the bottle is squashed and drives the water out. Without air there would be no pressure.
84167.m: A water rocket needs water and air.

84168.q: Which way does the bottle's opening point when a water rocket takes off?
84168.e: The bottle stands upside down on the launcher. That way the water sprays down and the bottle flies up.
84168.m: A water rocket stands upside down at launch.

84169.q: Why do you stick fins on a water rocket?
84169.e: Fins at the bottom keep the rocket stable. Without fins it would easily wobble.
84169.m: Fins make a rocket fly straight.

84170.q: What is important when launching a water rocket?
a: Looking straight down at the bottle
84170.e: The bottle shoots off very fast and can hurt someone. So you keep your distance and only launch it outside.
84170.m: Always keep your distance from a water rocket.

84171.q: Why does a water rocket fly higher if you pump more air into it?
a: Because the air cools the water
84171.e: More air means more pressure in the bottle. The water is forced out harder and the rocket is driven more strongly.
84171.m: The more pressure, the more powerfully the water rocket takes off.

84172.q: About how tall was the Saturn V Moon rocket?
84172.e: The Saturn V was around 110 metres tall. That is about as tall as a skyscraper with 35 floors.
84172.m: The Saturn V was as tall as a big skyscraper.

84173.q: How many stages did the Saturn V have?
84173.e: The Saturn V had three stages on top of each other. The Apollo spacecraft sat at the very top.
84173.m: The Saturn V was made of three stages.

84174.q: What happened to the first stage of the Saturn V when its fuel was used up?
a: It was dropped and fell into the sea
It flew all the way to the Moon
It landed back on the launch pad
It orbited the Earth for ever
84174.e: The empty first stage was separated after a few minutes. It crashed into the Atlantic while the upper stages flew on.
84174.m: The empty first stage of the Saturn V fell into the sea.

84175.q: Which engineer led the development of the Saturn V?
84175.e: Wernher von Braun was a German-American rocket engineer. His team developed the Saturn V.
84175.m: Wernher von Braun built the Saturn V with his team.

84176.q: In which decade did the Saturn V fly for the first time?
84176.e: The first flight of the Saturn V took place in 1967, still without people on board. The Moon flights followed.
84176.m: The Saturn V flew for the first time in 1967.

84177.q: How many astronauts flew towards the Moon on each Saturn V?
84177.e: Each Apollo spacecraft carried three astronauts. On the Moon landings, two went down to the Moon and one stayed in lunar orbit.
84177.m: Three astronauts flew on each Saturn V.

84178.q: Which space station did the last Saturn V carry into space in 1973?
84178.e: On its last launch, the Saturn V carried the American space station Skylab into orbit. It was the last flight of a Saturn V.
84178.m: The last Saturn V took the Skylab station into space.

84179.q: About how heavy was the Saturn V at launch?
84179.e: Fully fuelled, the Saturn V weighed almost 3000 tonnes. Most of that was fuel.
84179.m: The Saturn V was enormously heavy at launch.

a: A small rocket for hobbies and school
A firework for New Year's Eve
84180.e: Model rockets are small, light rockets that really fly. People build them as a hobby or in lessons.
84180.m: A model rocket is a small rocket you build yourself.

84181.q: How does a model rocket usually get back to the ground safely after its flight?
84181.e: A small parachute opens at the top. That way the rocket floats down slowly and can fly again.
84181.m: A parachute brings the model rocket back gently.

84182.q: How is a model rocket launched safely?
a: With a match right at the motor
With a lighter in your hand
84182.e: The motor is ignited with a cable and a switch. That way you stand far enough away.
84182.m: A model rocket is launched from a safe distance.

84183.q: How long does the motor of a model rocket burn?
84183.e: The motor is a small tube with solid fuel. It only burns for a few seconds, then the rocket flies on a bit further.
84183.m: A model rocket's motor burns only very briefly.

84184.q: What guides a model rocket at launch so it flies off straight?
84184.e: At launch the rocket slides along a thin metal rod. That way it flies in the right direction from the start.
84184.m: A launch rod guides the model rocket straight up.

84185.q: What are model rockets often made of?
84185.e: Model rockets have to be very light. So they are made of cardboard, balsa wood and plastic.
84185.m: A model rocket is made of light materials.

84186.q: Where is the best place to launch a model rocket?
84186.e: In an open field there are no obstacles and nothing can catch fire. And you can find the rocket again easily.
84186.m: Model rockets are launched in a wide, open field.

84187.q: Who should be there when children launch a model rocket?
84187.e: The small motor burns very hot. An adult helps and makes sure everything is safe.
84187.m: An adult helps when a model rocket is launched.

84188.q: Where do Ariane rockets take off?
84188.e: Ariane takes off from the European spaceport in Kourou. It lies on the north coast of South America.
84188.m: Ariane takes off in Kourou in South America.

84189.q: Which organisation is Ariane built for?
a: For the European Space Agency ESA
84189.e: Ariane is an ESA rocket. Switzerland is also a member of ESA.

84190.q: Which space telescope did an Ariane 5 carry into space in December 2021?
84190.e: On 25 December 2021, an Ariane 5 took off with the James Webb Telescope. It is one of the largest telescopes in space.
84190.m: An Ariane 5 took the James Webb Telescope into space.

84191.q: In which year did Ariane 6 fly for the first time?
84191.e: The first flight of Ariane 6 took place in July 2024. It replaces the older Ariane 5.
84191.m: Ariane 6 flew for the first time in 2024.

84192.q: Which part of Ariane is built by experts in Switzerland?
84192.e: The payload fairing is built in Emmen in the canton of Lucerne. This cover protects the satellites in the tip of the rocket.
84192.m: The tip of Ariane comes from Switzerland.

84193.q: Which figure from a Greek legend is Ariane named after?
84193.e: Ariane is the French form of the name Ariadne. In the legend, Ariadne helped the hero Theseus out of the labyrinth with a thread.
84193.m: The Ariane rocket bears the name of the legendary figure Ariadne.

84194.q: What does Ariane mostly carry into space?
84194.e: Ariane mainly transports satellites for television, weather and navigation. People do not fly on it.
84194.m: Ariane mainly takes satellites into space.

84195.q: Why did Europe build its own Ariane rockets?
a: To be able to launch satellites itself
To fly people to the Moon
84195.e: With Ariane, Europe does not have to wait for rockets from the USA or Russia. The first Ariane took off in 1979.
84195.m: With Ariane, Europe launches its own satellites into space.

84196.q: Which Ariane rocket flew from 1996 to 2023?
84196.e: Ariane 5 was in service for almost 30 years. Its last flight took place in July 2023.

84197.q: Which country does the Soyuz spacecraft come from?
84197.e: Soyuz was developed in the Soviet Union. Today it is built and flown by Russia.

84198.q: How many people fit in a Soyuz capsule?
84198.e: Three space travellers sit side by side in the cramped landing capsule. They wear their spacesuits.
84198.m: Three people fly in a Soyuz.

84199.q: Where do Soyuz spacecraft mostly fly to today?
84199.e: Soyuz takes space travellers to the International Space Station. Later it brings them back.
84199.m: Soyuz shuttles between the Earth and the space station.

84200.q: How does a Soyuz capsule land on Earth?
a: On a runway like an aeroplane
84200.e: The capsule floats down on large parachutes. It lands on the flat steppe.
84200.m: A Soyuz capsule lands on land using parachutes.

84201.q: Roughly how long have Soyuz spacecraft been flying?
84201.e: The first Soyuz flew in 1967. Since then the spacecraft has been improved again and again and is still flying today.
84201.m: Soyuz has been flying for over 50 years.

84202.q: In which country do Soyuz capsules normally land?
84202.e: Soyuz capsules land on the wide steppe of Kazakhstan. Recovery teams wait there with helicopters.
84202.m: Soyuz lands on the steppe of Kazakhstan.

84203.q: What fires shortly before a Soyuz capsule touches down, to slow it down?
84203.e: Just above the ground, small rockets fire. They make the landing softer.
84203.m: Braking rockets make the Soyuz landing gentler.

84204.q: Since which year have people flown into space in Soyuz spacecraft?
84204.e: The first crewed flight in a Soyuz took place in 1967. Since then the spacecraft has been improved again and again.

84205.q: What do you call a place from which rockets take off into space?
84205.e: A spaceport has launch pads, buildings and control centres. Rockets take off into space from there.
84205.m: Rockets take off from a spaceport.

84206.q: From which spaceport did Yuri Gagarin fly into space as the first person in 1961?
84206.e: Gagarin took off from Baikonur. It is the oldest spaceport in the world.
84206.m: The first person in space took off from Baikonur.

84207.q: In which US state is the Kennedy Space Center?
84207.e: The Kennedy Space Center is on the east coast of Florida. The Moon rockets took off from there.
84207.m: The Kennedy Space Center is in Florida.

84208.q: What is loaded into the rocket at the spaceport only shortly before launch?
84208.e: Many fuels are very cold or dangerous. That is why the tanks are only filled in the last few hours before launch.
84208.m: A rocket is only fuelled up shortly before launch.

84209.q: Why do people like to build spaceports close to the equator?
a: The Earth's rotation gives more momentum there
It is warmer there for astronauts
There are never any clouds there
84209.e: At the equator the ground turns fastest. The rocket gets this momentum for free.
84209.m: At the equator, the Earth's rotation helps a rocket at launch.

84210.q: Is there a spaceport in Switzerland?
84210.e: Switzerland has no spaceport. Swiss satellites take off from Kourou or from the USA, for example.
84210.m: Switzerland has no spaceport of its own.

84211.q: From which spaceport in South America do many European rockets take off?
84211.e: Kourou is in French Guiana, close to the equator. European rockets take off from there, including with Swiss satellites on board.
84211.m: Europe's rockets take off in Kourou in South America.

84212.q: Where are rockets assembled at a spaceport?
a: In a cave in a mountain
84212.e: In huge buildings the rocket parts are protected from rain and wind. Only when everything is finished is the rocket taken to the launch pad.
84212.m: Rockets are assembled in big buildings.

84213.q: Why does a rocket have to take oxygen with it?
a: Because there is no air in space for burning
84213.e: Without oxygen nothing can burn. There is no air in space, so the rocket has its own oxygen tank.
84213.m: A rocket brings its own oxygen.

84214.q: Which two substances burn in many large rockets?
84214.e: Liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen produce very powerful combustion. They are used in Ariane, for example.
84214.m: Many rockets burn hydrogen with oxygen.

84215.q: What is rocket fuel called that is hard, as in a firework rocket?
84215.e: Solid fuel is like a hard mass in the rocket tube. Once it has been lit, it burns to the end.
84215.m: Once lit, solid fuel burns to the end.

84216.q: What is produced when hydrogen burns with oxygen?
84216.e: Hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water. Because of the heat, it comes out of the nozzle as steam.

84217.q: How cold must liquid hydrogen be kept?
84217.e: Hydrogen only becomes liquid at about minus 253 degrees. So the tanks have to be very well insulated.

84218.q: What is the heaviest part of a rocket when it takes off?
84218.e: A rocket is mainly a giant tank. Almost all of its launch weight is fuel.
84218.m: Most of a rocket is fuel.

84219.q: Which fuel, also used by aeroplanes, burned in the first stage of the Saturn V?
84219.e: The first stage of the Saturn V burned kerosene together with liquid oxygen. Kerosene is also the fuel of jet aircraft.
84219.m: The first stage of the Saturn V ran on kerosene.

84220.q: What fuel is inside a firework rocket on Swiss National Day, 1 August?
84220.e: Firework rockets are powered by gunpowder. It burns quickly and drives the rocket upwards.

a: Because it quickly evaporates and disappears
84221.e: Rocket fuel contains a great deal of energy. A small mistake can lead to a fire or an explosion.
84221.m: Rocket fuel is very dangerous and is handled carefully.

84222.q: What does the term climate change mean?
a: The Earth's climate changes over a long time
The weather changes from one day to the next
84222.e: In climate change, the typical weather changes over many decades. Today the Earth is mainly getting warmer.
84222.m: Climate change means that the climate changes over a long time.

84223.q: Because of today's climate change, is the Earth getting warmer or colder on average?
84223.e: The Earth's average temperature has risen clearly over the last 150 years. That is why people also speak of global warming.
84223.m: Climate change is making the Earth warmer.

84224.q: Which human activity contributes especially strongly to climate change?
84224.e: Burning coal, oil and gas produces exhaust gases that hold heat in the air. This makes it warmer.
84224.m: Burning coal, oil and gas heats up the climate.

84226.q: What is an especially climate-friendly way to get to school?
84226.e: Walking or cycling produces no exhaust gases. It also keeps you fit.
84226.m: Walking or cycling is good for the climate.

84227.q: Because of climate change, what is happening to snow at low altitudes in Switzerland?
a: There is the same amount of snow
84227.e: Because it is warmer, rain falls more often instead of snow on the Central Plateau. Many low-lying ski areas are also short of snow.
84227.m: There is less snow in the lowlands today than in the past.

84228.q: Why do trees help against climate change?
a: They take carbon dioxide out of the air
84228.e: Trees need carbon dioxide to grow and store it in their wood. That way less of it stays in the air.
84228.m: Trees take carbon dioxide out of the air.

84229.q: How are heatwaves in Switzerland changing because of climate change?
a: They only come in winter now
84229.e: Because it is getting warmer overall, there are more very hot days. Heatwaves therefore happen more often and get stronger.
84229.m: With climate change there are more heatwaves.

84230.q: How can you save energy at home and so help the climate?
a: Switch off the light when you leave the room
Leave the windows open in winter
Leave the TV on all the time
84230.e: Electricity and heating use energy. If you switch off lights you do not need, you save energy.

84231.q: What are parts of the Rhône Glacier covered with in summer so that it melts more slowly?
84231.e: The white sheets reflect the sunlight. Underneath them the ice melts more slowly.
84231.m: White sheets protect the ice from the sun.

84232.q: Why are the glaciers in the Alps melting?
a: Because the wind is getting stronger
84232.e: In a warmer climate, more ice melts in summer than is added by snow in winter. That is why the glaciers are getting smaller.

84233.q: Where does the meltwater of a glacier flow?
84233.e: The meltwater gathers into streams. These flow into rivers such as the Rhône or the Rhine.
84233.m: Meltwater from glaciers flows into streams and rivers.

84234.q: What often forms where a glacier has melted away?
84234.e: Meltwater collects in the hollow that the ice leaves behind. This is how new glacier lakes form.
84234.m: Where a glacier disappears, a lake often forms.

84235.q: Why does ice covered in dark dust melt faster?
a: Dark surfaces absorb more heat from the sun
84235.e: Dark surfaces absorb more sunlight and so get warmer. That is why dirty ice melts faster.
84235.m: Dark surfaces get warmer in the sun than light ones.

84236.q: Which canton is the Great Aletsch Glacier in?
84236.e: The Great Aletsch Glacier is in Upper Valais. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
84236.m: The Aletsch Glacier is in Valais.

84237.q: In which season does the most glacier ice melt?
84237.e: In summer it is warm even in the mountains. That is when the most meltwater flows out of the glacier.

84238.q: What will be missing in high summer later on, once the glaciers have disappeared?
84238.e: Glaciers release a lot of water, especially in hot, dry summers. Without them, some rivers will then carry less water.
84238.m: Glaciers are important stores of water for the summer.

a: Several very hot days in a row
A high wave in the sea
A warm wind in the evening
84239.e: In a heatwave it stays very hot for several days. Often the nights hardly cool down either.
84239.m: A heatwave is lots of hot days in a row.

84240.q: What should you definitely do in great heat?
a: Run about in the sun at midday
84240.e: In heat, your body sweats out a lot of water. That is why you need to drink regularly, even if you are not thirsty.
84240.m: In hot weather, drink lots of water.

84241.q: Where was Switzerland's highest temperature, 41.5 °C in 2003, measured?
84241.e: On 11 August 2003, 41.5 °C was measured in Grono in the Misox valley. That is still the Swiss record today (as of 2026).
84241.m: The Swiss heat record comes from Grono.

84242.q: What is a day called when the temperature reaches at least 30 °C?
84242.e: From 30 °C, it is called a hot day. A summer day, on the other hand, only needs 25 °C.
84242.m: On a hot day it reaches at least 30 degrees.

84243.q: What is a night called when it does not cool down below 20 °C?
84243.e: On a tropical night it stays as warm as in the tropics. Many people sleep badly then.
84243.m: On a tropical night it stays above 20 degrees.

84244.q: Who is especially at risk during a heatwave?
84244.e: The bodies of babies and older people are less able to cool down. They need special attention in hot weather.
84244.m: Babies and older people need special protection in hot weather.

84245.q: On a hot summer's day, when is it usually hottest outside?
84245.e: The sun heats the ground and the air all day long. That is why it usually gets warmest in the afternoon.
84245.m: It is usually hottest outside in the afternoon.

84246.q: How do you keep a flat cool during the day in hot weather?
a: Open all the windows in the midday sun
84246.e: Closed shutters keep the sun out. It is best to air the rooms in the cool night or early morning.
84246.m: In hot weather, keep the shutters closed during the day.

84247.q: Which clothes are best in great heat?
84247.e: Light fabrics let air reach your skin, and pale colours heat up less. A hat also protects your head.
84247.m: In hot weather, wear light, pale clothes.

a: A long time with too little rain
84248.e: In a drought it rains too little for weeks or months. The soil, plants and rivers and lakes dry out.
84248.m: In a drought there is no rain for a long time.

84249.q: What do you often see in the ground during a drought?
84249.e: When the soil dries out, it shrinks. This makes cracks.
84249.m: In dry weather, the ground cracks.

84250.q: Why are fires in the forest often banned in very dry weather?
a: Because a forest fire can start quickly
Because the trees are asleep then
Because otherwise it starts to rain
Because the foresters are on holiday
84250.e: Dry leaves and grass burn very easily. One spark can start a big forest fire.
84250.m: In dry weather, do not light fires in the forest.

84251.q: In the drought summer of 2018, how did some cows on Swiss alpine pastures get water?
a: The army flew it in by helicopter
They licked ice from the glaciers
They drank milk instead of water
84251.e: Because springs dried up, the Swiss Army flew water up to alpine pastures by helicopter. That way the animals had enough to drink.
84251.m: In summer 2018 the army flew water to the cows.

84252.q: What happens to the plants in the fields during a drought?
84252.e: Plants need water to live. Without rain they wilt and the harvest is small.

84253.q: What happens to the water in rivers and lakes during a long dry spell?
84253.e: Without rain, less water flows in. That is why rivers and lakes get lower.
84253.m: In dry weather the water level drops.

84254.q: Why do fish in streams suffer during a drought?
a: The water gets scarce and too warm
84254.e: Shallow, warm water has less oxygen. But many fish, such as trout, need cool water.

84255.q: How can you save water in the garden in dry weather?
a: Collect rainwater and use it for watering
Leave the sprinkler on all day
Water at midday in the blazing sun
Refill the paddling pool every day
84255.e: With collected rainwater you do not need to use tap water. Watering in the evening also saves water.
84255.m: Collected rainwater helps to save water.

84256.q: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
84256.e: The Sahara is roughly as big as the USA. It is the largest hot desert on Earth.
84256.m: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world.

84257.q: Which animal can go a long time without water in the desert?
84257.e: Camels can go many days without drinking. They store fat in their hump.
84257.m: The camel can manage a long time without water.

84258.q: What is a place with water and palm trees in the middle of the desert called?
84258.e: In an oasis, groundwater comes to the surface. Date palms grow there and people can live there.
84258.m: An oasis is a green place with water in the desert.

84259.q: What is it often like at night in a sandy desert?
a: Just as hot as at midday
84259.e: Because there are hardly any clouds, the heat escapes quickly at night. That is why it often gets cold in the desert at night.
84259.m: It can get cold in the desert at night.

84260.q: What is the illusion called when you seem to see water in the distance in the hot desert?
84260.e: Hot air above the ground bends the light. You then see the sky reflected, and it looks like a lake.
84260.m: A mirage tricks you into seeing water in the desert.

84261.q: Which desert in Chile is one of the driest in the world?
84261.e: In parts of the Atacama no rain falls for years. It lies in South America on the Pacific coast.
84261.m: The Atacama in Chile is extremely dry.

84262.q: Which plant in American deserts stores water in its thick stem?
84262.e: Cacti store water in their fleshy stem. Their spines protect them from animals.
84262.m: A cactus stores water in its stem.

84263.q: Why is Antarctica also considered a desert?
a: Because very little precipitation falls there
Because it is made of sand
Because it is very hot there
84263.e: A desert is an area with very little precipitation. Only a little snow falls in Antarctica, so it is a cold desert.
84263.m: An icy region can be a desert too.

84264.q: On which continent is most of the Amazon rainforest?
84264.e: Most of it is in Brazil. Peru, Colombia and other countries also have a share of it.
84264.m: The Amazon rainforest is in South America.

84265.q: Which slow animal hangs upside down from branches in the rainforest?
84265.e: Sloths move very slowly and hang from branches by their long claws. They sleep many hours a day.
84265.m: The sloth hangs comfortably upside down in the tree.

84266.q: Why are many rainforests cut down?
a: To make room for fields and pastures
To make room for ski slopes
So that the animals have more light
84266.e: Rainforest is cleared to sell the timber and to create fields or cattle pastures. Many animals lose their habitat as a result.
84266.m: When rainforest is cut down, animals lose their home.

84267.q: What is the weather like in the tropical rainforest all year round?
84267.e: The tropical rainforest lies close to the equator. There it is warm all year and the air is humid.
84267.m: In the tropical rainforest it is always warm and humid.

84268.q: Which plants climb up trees in the rainforest?
84268.e: Lianas climb up tree trunks towards the light. Some animals use them like ropes.
84268.m: Lianas climb up trees in the rainforest.

84269.q: Where in the rainforest do most kinds of animals live?
84269.e: In the treetops there is lots of light, flowers and fruit. That is why especially many kinds of animals live there.
84269.m: The treetops of the rainforest are teeming with animals.

84270.q: Is there solid land under the North Pole?
a: No, there is sea with ice on top
84270.e: The North Pole lies in the middle of the Arctic Ocean. The ice on it floats on the water.
84270.m: Under the North Pole there is sea, not land.

84271.q: Which big white predator lives in the Arctic?
84271.e: The polar bear is one of the largest predators on land. Its thick fur keeps it warm.
84271.m: The polar bear lives in the Arctic.

84272.q: Roughly which direction does the needle of a compass point?
84272.e: The compass needle is a small magnet. It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field and points roughly north.

84273.q: What is it called when the sun shines even at midnight in the Arctic summer?
84273.e: In summer, close to the pole, the sun does not set for days. You can even see it at midnight.
84273.m: In the Arctic summer there is the midnight sun.

84274.q: Roughly how long does it stay dark exactly at the North Pole in winter?
84274.e: At the North Pole the sun rises only once a year and sets once. That is why day and night there each last about half a year.
84274.m: At the North Pole the night lasts half a year.

84275.q: Which people have lived in the Arctic for a long time, for example in Greenland?
84275.e: The Inuit have lived in the far north for centuries. In the past they hunted mainly seals and whales.
84275.m: The Inuit live in the Arctic.

84276.q: Which animals with antlers roam the Arctic in big herds?
84276.e: Reindeer travel in big herds across the tundra. In North America they are called caribou.
84276.m: Reindeer roam the far north in herds.

84277.q: Who was the first to reach the South Pole, in 1911?
84277.e: The Norwegian Roald Amundsen reached the South Pole with dog sleds on 14 December 1911. The Briton Robert Scott arrived about a month later.
84277.m: Roald Amundsen was the first at the South Pole.

84278.q: Which birds live in Antarctica but cannot fly?
84278.e: Penguins are excellent swimmers. Their wings have become flippers.
84278.m: Penguins cannot fly, but they are great swimmers.

84279.q: Are there polar bears in Antarctica?
a: Yes, but only on the coast
84279.e: Polar bears only live in the far north. There are none in Antarctica.
84279.m: There are no polar bears in Antarctica.

84280.q: How thick is the ice on Antarctica at its thickest points?
84280.e: At its thickest points, the ice sheet is over 4000 metres thick. That is higher than most Alpine summits.
84280.m: The ice on Antarctica is kilometres thick.

a: Only scientists in research stations, for a while
Nobody, no one may ever set foot there
84281.e: Antarctica has no permanent residents. Scientists live there in research stations for a few months.
84281.m: Only scientists live in Antarctica, for a while.

84282.q: Where was the lowest air temperature on Earth measured?
84282.e: In 1983, -89.2 °C was measured at Vostok Station in Antarctica. That is a world record.
84282.m: Antarctica is the coldest place on Earth.

84283.q: How much of an iceberg can you see above the water?
84283.e: Most of an iceberg lies under water. You only see the tip.
84283.m: You only see the tip of an iceberg.

84284.q: Is an iceberg made of salt water or fresh water?
84284.e: The ice of an iceberg formed from snow, not from frozen seawater. That is why it is not salty.
84284.m: Icebergs are made of fresh water.

84285.q: What is it called when a big piece of ice breaks off a glacier into the sea?
84285.e: In calving, a block of ice breaks off the glacier and crashes into the sea. This is how a new iceberg forms.
84285.m: When a glacier calves, an iceberg forms.

84286.q: Where do most big icebergs come from?
a: From glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica
84286.e: Big glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica flow all the way to the sea. Icebergs break off there.
84286.m: Most icebergs come from Greenland and Antarctica.

84287.q: What happens to an iceberg that drifts into warmer water?
84287.e: In warmer water the ice melts bit by bit. In the end nothing is left.
84287.m: An iceberg melts in warm water.

84288.q: What colour can very old, dense ice in an iceberg be?
